roles.title: Locomotive Engineers
roles.description: Drive electric, diesel-electric, steam, or gas-turbine-electric locomotives to transport passengers or freight. Interpret train orders, electronic or manual signals, and railroad rules and regulations.

tasks.label: Receive starting signals from conductors and use controls such as throttles or air brakes to drive electric, diesel-electric, steam, or gas turbine-electric locomotives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Class I road freight: engineer takes charge of a 6,000-14,000 ft mainline train after the conductor's air-test/highball, then drives it 100-300 miles over signalled/PTC territory — throttle, dynamic and air brake handling on grades, slack management, speed-restriction and wayside-signal compliance, grade crossings, weather, meets in sidings.

Yard/terminal engineer in a classification or flat-switching yard: repeated short moves building and breaking trains, responding continuously to a ground crew's hand or radio signals, coupling, shoving blind cuts, spotting to a stop within a car length, hand-thrown switches, people on the ground.

Local/way freight and industrial switching: run out on the branch, then switch several customer plants and spurs — shoving into unfamiliar industry tracks, street/private crossings, derails and hand-thrown switches, conductor giving start/stop signals by radio and hand.

Commuter or intercity passenger run (Amtrak, Metra, MARC-type): depart on the conductor's highball, drive over shared mainline with grade crossings and mixed freight traffic, precise platform stops on time, signal and speed-restriction compliance with passengers aboard.

Short line or regional freight over lightly signalled or dark territory under track warrants/verbal authority: slower speeds, jointed or lower-class track, many public crossings in small towns, short trains, frequent stops for setouts.

Captive industrial, port or mine railroad: repetitive unit-train and cut movements inside a plant, coal/ore terminal or port complex — loop tracks, loadouts, dumpers, spotting under chutes, on private institution-controlled trackage.

tasks.label: Inspect locomotives to verify adequate fuel, sand, water, or other supplies before each run or to check for mechanical problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Class I freight road engineer, pre-departure daily inspection of a 2-3 unit locomotive consist on a departure/service track at a terminal: walk each unit at ground level checking trucks, wheels, brake rigging, safety appliances and fluid leaks; read the fuel gauge on the tank, confirm sand is filled, check water/oil sight glasses in the engine compartment; mount into the cab to check gauges, alerter, event recorder, headlights/ditch lights, horn, wipers and cab supplies; test sanders and brakes; sign off / report defects. Outdoors on ballast, day or night, any weather.

Yard or local switching engineer taking charge of a switcher or road-switcher at a small yard or engine house: unit is often already running; check fuel level, sand, water and oil, look over trucks and running gear for mechanical problems, check cab equipment and supplies, note defects before beginning work. Rough ballast footing, congested track area, all weather.

Passenger/commuter engineer's pre-departure check of a locomotive or cab car at a coach yard, maintenance facility or station platform: cab equipment and control checks, brake test, exterior walk-around for leaks and damaged components, verification that fuel/water/supplies are adequate for the assignment, defect reporting to the mechanical department.

Mechanical-condition check only, of a locomotive or locomotive consist at a terminal where the units can be pulled slowly past a fixed inspection point or spotted on a service track: look for defective running gear, worn or missing brake shoes, dragging or loose components, and fluid leaks on the exterior/underframe; produce a defect report. No cab or supply items involved.

En-route or field inspection: engineer stops and inspects the locomotive after an alarm or symptom (loss of load, low air, wheel slip / no sand, hot engine, smell or noise) at a siding, industry track, or on the mainline in open country; climbs down onto uneven ballast, walks the unit, opens compartment doors, checks levels and looks for the fault, in whatever weather, terrain and lighting are present.

tasks.label: Operate locomotives to transport freight or passengers between stations or to assemble or disassemble trains within rail yards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Class I / regional road freight: operate a manifest, unit or intermodal train between terminals over signaled mainline for an 8-12 hour tour - starting and stopping heavy tonnage on grades, obeying wayside/cab signals and PTC, handling meets, slow orders, grade crossings, night and adverse weather.

Yard switching: assemble and disassemble trains in a flat or hump classification yard - pulling cuts, shoving into bowl tracks, doubling over, coupling to standing cars, spotting for air tests, working to a conductor's radio/hand signals over a full shift.

Local/way freight and industrial switching: run a local or short-line job, switching customer plants, mines, elevators and port spurs - tight clearances, private and unprotected crossings, poorly maintained industry track, trucks/forklifts/pedestrians on the property, layout differing at every customer.

Scheduled passenger service: operate a commuter or intercity train between stations - precise platform stops, station dwell and door coordination, tight schedule adherence, station-area pedestrians and grade crossings.

Hostling and terminal moves: move light locomotives and consists around engine terminals, fuel pads, service and ready tracks and stabling sidings; couple power onto outbound trains and move equipment to/from shops.

tasks.label: Respond to emergency conditions or breakdowns, following applicable safety procedures and rules.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mainline hazard requiring an immediate emergency stop with no contact: vehicle or trespasser at a crossing, debris or an obstruction ahead, a stop indication or an emergency radio call. Engineer sounds the horn, places the brake in emergency, stops the train, notifies the dispatcher, confirms the train is intact, recharges the air and proceeds. Work is done from the cab; day or night, all weather, freight or passenger.

Undesired emergency brake application or train separation en route: the air dumps and the train stops on the road. Crew secures the train, walks the consist (often a mile or more of ballast, brush, bridges, grade crossings, in whatever weather and terrain the train stopped in), finds the broken air hose, parted knuckle or dragging equipment, makes the repair or re-couples, recharges the brake pipe, performs the required brake test and resumes.

Locomotive breakdown en route: prime mover shutdown, load loss, ground relay, PCS open, air compressor or dynamic brake failure. Engineer follows the troubleshooting guide, resets breakers and relays in the electrical cabinet and engine compartment, restarts the engine, isolates the unit or sets it up dead-in-tow, reports to the dispatcher and mechanical desk, and continues at reduced power or requests a rescue engine.

Serious emergency at the scene: grade-crossing collision, striking a trespasser, derailment, on-board fire or hazmat release. Emergency stop, protection of adjacent tracks, notification of dispatcher and 911, securing the train, walking inspection for damage and derailed equipment, briefing responders and remaining on scene under the rules. Involves public roadway and off-right-of-way ground.

Yard or terminal emergency/breakdown: broken knuckle or air hose while switching, sticking brakes, a car fouling or picking a switch at low speed. Stop the movement, protect it, cut out or set out the car, change the knuckle, set and release handbrakes, retest the air and continue. Occurs on railroad-controlled yard tracks with standard equipment and lighting.

Passenger-train emergency (commuter or intercity): passenger medical emergency or emergency alarm, door or head-end-power fault, smoke alarm. Bring the train to a controlled stop or run to the next station platform, coordinate with the conductor and the control center, hold and secure the train while responders attend, then restore and resume or await a rescue move.

sources.system: Siemens ATC driverless U-Bahn (RUBIN), Nuremberg U2/U3
sources.title: Nuremberg Automatic U-Bahn - Railway Technology
sources.claim: Nuremberg's driverless U2/U3 metro lines (in public service since 2008, sharing track with manually driven trains and without platform screen doors) automatically make an emergency stop when a track obstruction is detected and alert the CCTV-equipped control centre, i.e. the machine performs the driver's hazard-stop-and-report response.
sources.transferJustification: Same task element as the engineer's response to a hazard on the track: detect the emergency condition, make an emergency brake application, and report to the controlling authority, on a rail system carrying revenue trains.

sources.title: Driverless rail vehicles – Safe and driverless public transport – Fraunhofer IKS
sources.claim: Independent confirmation that the Nuremberg driverless lines' track-bed obstacle detection automatically brakes the train, while noting that fully unattended operation still depends on human support.
sources.transferJustification: Corroborates the automatic emergency-braking response to a hazard (the in-cab part of this task) and documents the limit: human staff remain necessary for the rest of incident handling.

sources.system: Skyline (Honolulu rail transit), Hitachi Rail driverless CBTC
sources.title: How Hitachi and Honolulu Are Writing a New Page in the History of Mass Transportation
sources.claim: Honolulu's Skyline is a driverless GoA4 mass-transit railway in revenue service in the US; on-board and wayside emergencies are handled by the automatic train system plus a remote control center that coordinates with first responders, with no operator on the train.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the train-handling and notification role an engineer performs in a passenger emergency: the automated train stops and the remote control center notifies responders; physical care of passengers is other staff's job.

sources.system: Copenhagen Metro (driverless, Ansaldo/Hitachi CBTC), operated by Metro Service
sources.title: Metro Service has operated a driverless metro for 20 years
sources.claim: The Copenhagen Metro has run driverless in revenue service for over 20 years, but human stewards must board and drive trains manually when needed and technicians maintain and repair the fleet - the automation does not itself recover a failed train.
sources.transferJustification: Shows the fallback for breakdowns and degraded conditions on the most mature unattended railway is a human who boards and drives, not an autonomous recovery.

sources.title: World-first autonomous trains deployed at Rio Tinto's iron ore operations
sources.claim: Rio Tinto's AutoHaul operates driverless heavy-haul freight trains over a 1,700 km private mainline with public level crossings, monitored remotely from an operations centre - the most mature autonomous mainline freight operation.

sources.system: Rio Tinto autonomous iron ore trains (AutoHaul network)
sources.title: Autonomous ore train involved in collision in Australia - Trains
sources.claim: When an autonomous AutoHaul-type ore train was disabled by a ... in the Pilbara, human workers were sent out to repair the disabled train and a recovery train was dispatched (which then collided with it) - autonomous mainline freight does not self-diagnose, self-repair or self-recover from a breakdown.

tasks.label: Check to ensure that brake examination tests are conducted at shunting stations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Inspect locomotives after runs to detect damaged or defective equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Road freight engineer ties up at a terminal: walk-around inspection of the locomotive consist on a yard servicing/arrival track — looking for fuel/oil/water leaks, damaged or worn brake shoes and rigging, wheel or truck damage, loose/missing parts, damaged steps, handrails, plow, hoses and couplers — and writing the defects on the locomotive condition report / F6180-49A.

Cab and onboard-equipment portion of the post-run check at tie-up: verifying and reporting condition of speed indicator, alerter/PTC screen, cab signals, event recorder, headlights/ditch lights, horn and bell, wipers, sanders, cab heat/AC, seats and windows — operating controls to confirm faults noticed during the run, then tagging/writing up the unit.

Yard, local or short-line engineer inspects the unit at end of shift on an engine-house track or small service track: walk-by for leaks and damage, checks sand level and fuel gauge, looks at running gear, often at night on older non-standard power.

Post-run inspection at an outlying tie-up point — main-line crew-change location, industrial siding or customer track with no facilities: engineer walks the ballast beside the unit in the dark, rain, snow or heat, with only a lantern, to check for damage before leaving it.

Passenger/commuter engineer at a terminal or layover facility: post-run inspection of the locomotive or cab car — exterior condition, brake rigging, HEP and coupler/diaphragm condition — and hand-off of a defect report to the mechanical department.

Follow-up inspection of a specific fault that occurred en route (traction motor smell, ground relay, wheel slide flat spot, dragging equipment): locating and evaluating the damaged component, sometimes opening engine-room or electrical-cabinet doors, and deciding whether the unit must be isolated or set out.

sources.title: Intelligent Robot for Under Train Maintenance and Inspection
sources.claim: Shenhao's TVIS2000 is a wheeled mobile robot with a robotic arm that navigates autonomously in metro depots, images key under-vehicle and train-side inspection points and automatically classifies faults, replacing the manual nightly visual daily inspection of subway vehicles; claimed average fault recognition rate above 98%.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: the depot 'daily inspection' of rail vehicles after service. Same objects (bogies, brake gear, underframe, train sides), same defect classes (cracked/broken/loose parts, leaks, wear) and same institution-controlled depot setting as a locomotive engineer's post-run walkaround.

sources.developer: Boston Dynamics / Energy Robotics for Deutsche Bahn
sources.title: Erstmals im Praxistest: Roboterhund „Spot“ im Einsatz für digitale Instandhaltung von Güterwagen
sources.claim: Deutsche Bahn ran Boston Dynamics' Spot (software by Energy Robotics) at DB Cargo's Mainz-Bischofsheim maintenance works, where the robot independently identifies freight wagons and performs visual inspections to detect damage, including wheelset-axle visual inspection from the maintenance pit; DB states it removes the need for pit work under the train.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: post-run visual damage inspection of rail rolling stock in a maintenance works. Same vehicle class, same visual defect types (cracks, wear, damage on running gear) and the same kind of institution-controlled rail facility a locomotive is tied up at.

sources.title: Transforming Rail Operations Through Automated Robotic Inspection
sources.claim: ANYbotics' ANYmal legged robot ran autonomous inspection missions at railCare's Domat/Ems rail freight facility, using high-resolution cameras and sensors to detect small cracks and wear on wagon wheel axles.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: visual/sensor inspection of rail vehicles for defects at a rail facility; comparable objects (wheelsets, running gear) and precision (hairline cracks) to the defect-finding an engineer does on a post-run walkaround.

sources.title: Autonomous Detection of Combustible Gas Leaks
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot is commercially deployed for routine autonomous inspection rounds in large industrial facilities, navigating a 40-acre midstream gas plant to perform anomaly detection, thermal inspection, gauge reading and combustible-gas leak detection; Orbit software plans and manages the recurring missions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repeatable walk-the-route equipment inspection inside a structured human work facility — traversing to fixed inspection points, spotting leaks and abnormal conditions and reading gauges — which is the traverse-and-perceive core of a post-run locomotive walkaround.

sources.system: E-Check (camera arch + MUFIG mobile underfloor unit + E-Check cobots)
sources.developer: Deutsche Bahn with Gestalt Robotics, Strama-MPS, Götting, Basler
sources.title: E-Check of ICE Trains: Automated inspection with mobile robot, 32 ace 2 cameras, and AI
sources.claim: Deutsche Bahn's E-Check at the Cologne-Nippes ICE plant inspects trains as they arrive in the maintenance hall using a 32-camera arch, a mobile underfloor inspection unit (AGV-based) and two-armed mobile cobots; DB describes it as a semi-automated, hybrid system in which humans stay in the maintenance loop.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: inspecting a train for defects on arrival at the depot after a run — the passenger-rail equivalent of the post-run locomotive inspection, in an institution-controlled maintenance hall.

sources.developer: Boston Dynamics / Energy Robotics for Deutsche Bahn
sources.title: Spotty the robot aids DB train maintenance
sources.claim: Deutsche Bahn deployed quadruped inspection robots ('Spotty', Boston Dynamics + Energy Robotics) in maintenance workshops in Munich and Cologne that visually inspect under trains and on train roofs to detect faults, working alongside a camera portal that scans trains entering the depot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: workshop fault-detection inspection of rail vehicles after service; corroborates the depot-inspection deployments above (autonomy not stated in this source, so treated as corroboration only).

sources.system: Digital Train Inspection Portal (Machine Vision Inspection)
sources.developer: Norfolk Southern / Georgia Tech Research Institute
sources.title: Norfolk Southern deploys second Digital Train Inspection portal in Georgia
sources.claim: Norfolk Southern operates fixed Digital Train Inspection Portals (with GTRI) that photograph and AI-screen passing trains for mechanical defects at up to 70 mph; the portals are purpose-built trackside installations and NS positions them as augmenting, not replacing, human inspectors, with flagged data reviewed by experts at its operations center.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated detection of mechanical defects on rail equipment; it is a fixed machine-vision installation rather than a mobile robot, so it is cited only as supporting evidence for work brought to a purpose-built inspection station (E1).

tasks.label: Monitor train loading procedures to ensure that freight or rolling stock are loaded or unloaded without damage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Unit-train bulk loading at a producer's loadout (coal mine flood loader, grain shuttle elevator, frac-sand or aggregate plant, ethanol/crude rack): the engineer creeps the train through the loading shed at roughly 0.5-1 mph on radio/telemetry cues from the loadout operator, keeps each car spotted under the spout, watches for overfill, spillage, mis-spots and damage to cars, and stops the movement if loading goes wrong.

Unit-train unloading at a receiving terminal (power-plant or port rotary dumper, bottom-dump pit at an elevator, tank-car unloading rack): the engineer shoves or indexes the train through the dumper/pit in coordination with the facility, monitors that cars are emptied, doors/gates operated and cars not damaged, and repositions the consist as unloading proceeds.

Local/industrial job spotting cars at customer facilities (lumber yard, steel or plastics plant, scrap dealer, warehouse dock, transload site) and staying to watch loading/unloading by the customer's forklifts, cranes or loaders: verifying correct spot, clearance, that lading and cars are not damaged, and pulling or re-spotting cars as loading proceeds.

Intermodal ramp or finished-vehicle facility: the engineer positions cuts of well cars, spine cars or auto racks under cranes/side loaders or at loading ramps and monitors containers, trailers or automobiles being loaded/unloaded and secured without damage to lading or rolling stock.

Post-loading / pre-departure condition check of the loaded train in a yard or at an industry: rolling by or walking the consist to spot shifted, leaning or improperly secured loads, open hatches or doors, overloaded or high-wide cars, and dunnage or banding failures before the train departs.

sources.developer: Rio Tinto with Hitachi Rail STS
sources.title: Rise of the machines: Rio Tinto breaks new ground with AutoHaul - International Railway Journal
sources.claim: Rio Tinto's AutoHaul driverless heavy-haul system in the Pilbara runs iron-ore trains with no crew on board, and the loading and unloading of product ... likewise automated, i.e. no engineer monitors the load-out or the port dumper.

sources.developer: Rio Tinto with Hitachi Rail STS
sources.title: AutoHaul Drives Efficiencies at Rio Tinto in Australia - Railway Track and Structures
sources.claim: As of 2026 Rio Tinto runs up to 53 simultaneous GoA4 driverless trains; on arrival at the mine the train itself switches into an automated loading mode that fills all 244 wagons before resuming mainline running, replacing the engineer's creep-loading and load monitoring.

sources.title: Automation | Rio Tinto
sources.claim: Rio Tinto describes AutoHaul as the world's first heavy-haul long-distance ... over ~1,700 km with about 200 locomotives, with automated responses to alarms - i.e. the automation, not a crew, reacts to abnormal conditions on a privately controlled but human-used industrial railway.

sources.system: Vollert KR 100 shunting robot with automatic loading station
sources.title: Loading gravel fully automatically and environmentally friendly - Vollert
sources.claim: At Eqiom's Bar-sur-Aube quarry a Vollert KR 100 shunting robot pulls wagons continuously through a fully automatic gravel filling station with automated weighing and real-time target/actual correction - the machine equivalent of the engineer creep-loading a train and watching for over/under-loading.

sources.system: Vollert DER100 / PRO DER100 shunting robot
sources.title: Press center | Vollert Heavy Duty Solutions
sources.claim: Vollert's fully automatic DER100 shunting robot performs automated railcar loading of ballast ..., autonomously positioning and moving the railcars inside the loading facility; a comparable PRO DER100 moves car groups through the loading area at Suzano's pulp site.

sources.system: Metso rotary railcar dumpers and train positioners
sources.title: Rotary railcar dumpers and train positioners (brochure)
sources.claim: Rotary railcar dumper installations use over-the-coupler train positioners that index coupled unit-train cars through the dumper automatically at high rates, mechanising the car spotting and repositioning the engineer performs during bulk unloading.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanised indexing/spotting of cars through an unloading station is the positioning-and-monitoring half of the engineer's unloading duty; same cars, same tolerances, same facility.

sources.title: CargoBeamer opens Calais intermodal terminal - Railway Gazette International
sources.claim: CargoBeamer's Calais terminal, a purpose-built transhipment facility, opened and transfers road semi-trailers to and from ... using automated transhipment modules rather than crews and cranes.

sources.title: Cargobeamer to launch Calais intermodal service - Lloyd's Loading List
sources.claim: The Calais facility is equipped with automated transhipment modules that load a complete train of semi-trailers in about 20 minutes, with the pallets pre-loaded away from the train, removing the human monitoring of each trailer being placed on a wagon.

sources.title: Intermodal terminals are moving towards semi-automation and/or full automation (Port Technology International)
sources.claim: Crane builder Kuenz notes that intermodal rail transfer yards cannot be fenced off for unmanned automation the way container stacks are, because loads may never be swung over people, locomotives and trucks - a constraint on fully automatic train loading in ordinary human-staffed intermodal terminals.

sources.title: Autonomous mobility: The future of rail is automated | Alstom
sources.claim: Alstom has demonstrated a fully autonomous shunting locomotive with obstacle detection and ATO in the Netherlands - yard-level autonomous car handling exists only as demonstration, not as deployed service at customer industries.

sources.title: FRA approves first autonomous railcar test program - FreightWaves
sources.claim: US autonomous freight rail outside private mining networks is still at pilot stage: FRA approved Parallel Systems' first autonomous railcar test programme on two Georgia short lines in 2025.

tasks.label: Drive diesel-electric rail-detector cars to transport rail-flaw-detecting machines over tracks.

roles.title: Rail Yard Engineers, Dinkey Operators, and Hostlers
roles.description: Drive switching or other locomotive or dinkey engines within railroad yard, industrial plant, quarry, construction project, or similar location.

tasks.label: Observe and respond to wayside and cab signals, including color light signals, position signals, torpedoes, flags, and hot box detectors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Flat-switching in a Class I or regional railroad classification yard: the engineer works a cut of cars with a ground crew, watching for hand/lantern signals and radio direction, dwarf and yard signals, blue-flag protection on tracks with workers, derails and switch targets, and responding by starting, slowing, spotting and stopping the locomotive at low speed among other movements.

In-plant/dinkey switching at an industrial plant, mine, quarry, grain or transload facility or port terminal: moving loaded/empty cars between loadouts, dumpers and interchange tracks on private industrial trackage, responding to plant signal lights, gate/loadout indications, flags and stop signs, and hand signals from plant personnel.

Hostling at an engine terminal/servicing facility: moving light locomotives between ready tracks, fuel pad, wash rack and shop, obeying dwarf signals, shop derails and blue-flag protection, and hand signals from shop and fueling staff.

Transfer and local runs over signaled main or industrial lead track between yards or to customers: observing wayside color-light and position-light signals and cab signal indications, complying with restricting/approach aspects and temporary speed restriction flags, and acting on wayside defect (hot box/dragging equipment) detector broadcasts, including stopping for an alarm.

Dinkey/locomotive operation on temporary or ad hoc trackage at a construction project, tunnel drive, or quarry expansion: muck or material trains on track that shifts as work advances, direction given by hand signals, lamps and flags from the shift boss, no fixed signal system.

sources.developer: Rio Tinto with Hitachi Rail STS
sources.title: AutoHaul Drives Efficiencies at Rio Tinto in Australia — Railway Track and Structures
sources.claim: Rio Tinto's AutoHaul operates driverless (GoA4) heavy-haul trains at scale across a 2,000 km private rail network in the Pilbara, the trains running under a Hitachi Rail signalling/train-control system rather than a human reading signals.

sources.title: Heavy Haul Freight Transportation System: AutoHaul — Hitachi Review
sources.claim: AutoHaul automatically stops the train in response to wayside detector alarms such as hot bearing and dragging equipment detectors, and to critical wayside equipment failures — the automated equivalent of an engineer responding to a hot box detector.

sources.title: Automation — Rio Tinto
sources.claim: Rio Tinto states AutoHaul makes automated responses to speed restrictions ... and reduces risk at level crossings on its ~1,700 km Pilbara network of about 200 locomotives.

sources.system: Alstom ATO GoA4 shunting locomotive with NIART/Elta ODS
sources.title: Alstom demonstrates fully autonomous driving of a shunting locomotive in the Netherlands
sources.claim: Alstom, ProRail and Lineas demonstrated a shunting locomotive running at GoA4 near Breda on Dutch rail infrastructure, with ATO plus an obstacle detection and recognition system handling starting, driving, stopping and unforeseen obstacles with no staff aboard.
sources.transferJustification: Shunting/switching movement control is the same act as responding to a movement signal in a yard: the ATO takes the movement authority and executes start/slow/stop at the same speeds and precision a yard engineer uses.

sources.system: DB Cargo automated hump shunting locomotive (Railergy/Bosch/ITK)
sources.developer: DB Cargo AG with Bosch Engineering and ITK Engineering
sources.title: DB Cargo and Bosch subsidiaries develop fully automated shunting locomotive for series production
sources.claim: DB Cargo, with Bosch Engineering and ITK Engineering, has trialled a prototype fully automated hump shunting locomotive in the working Munich North marshalling yard, with GoA4 series deployment planned after regulatory approval expected end-2027.
sources.transferJustification: Hump shunting is signal/authority-driven locomotive movement inside a working yard; the onboard automation performs the observe-and-respond loop (authority, speed limits, stop points) that the task describes.

sources.title: Intramotev, Austria's ÖBB Forge TugVolt Commercial Agreement — Railway Age
sources.claim: Intramotev's TugVolt self-propelled autonomous railcars are in revenue service performing industrial rail movements at a Carmeuse limestone mine in Michigan, with further commercial deployments at a Watco transload terminal in Illinois and on R.J. Corman's Memphis Line for industrial switching.
sources.transferJustification: Industrial switching by a crewless self-propelled car requires the same observe-and-respond movement control (permission to move, speed limits, stop points, crossings) that a dinkey operator performs on plant trackage.

sources.title: U.S. Army tests robot railcar to move military cargo — Defence Blog
sources.claim: TugVolt was used as a switcher to reposition DODX railcars between rail spurs at Camp Shelby during a June 2026 US Army exercise; the vendor describes the kit as supporting either remote-controlled or fully autonomous ..., so the autonomy of this particular event is not established.
sources.transferJustification: Spotting and repositioning cars between spurs is the physical response a hostler/switching engineer makes to movement signals; cited only as context, not as a positive-capability basis.

sources.title: CSX seeks FRA approval to use Trip Optimizer's automatic start and stop feature — Trains
sources.claim: Wabtec's Trip Optimizer runs US Class I freight trains under automatic throttle and dynamic brake control over millions of miles annually; its Zero-to-Zero function takes signal aspects and authorities from PTC and automatically starts and stops the train, and CSX is seeking FRA approval to use it.

sources.title: Conductors' union opposes CSX proposal to use Trip Optimizer's automatic start and stop feature — Trains
sources.claim: Reported limits of Zero-to-Zero: it cannot run a train automatically where there are no signals, ... in yards, or where a stop within half the range of vision is required.

sources.system: LKAB Kiruna underground automatic railway (Bombardier INTERFLO 150 CBTC)
sources.title: Signalling down the mine — Rail Engineer
sources.claim: LKAB's Kiruna underground iron-ore mine runs driverless ore trains on a standard-gauge underground railway controlled by Bombardier's INTERFLO 150 CBTC system, in continuous production use.
sources.transferJustification: Hauling ore trains underground on a fixed industrial layout is the same movement-control task as a dinkey operator hauling muck/material: the CBTC delivers the signal indications and the train responds automatically.

sources.title: Automated standard-gauge mine railway opens in Kiruna, Sweden — International Railway Journal
sources.claim: A 12 km standard-gauge underground automatic railway was inaugurated at LKAB's Kiruna mine at the 1,365 m level as part of the mine's production system.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: automated underground ore haulage substitutes for a dinkey operator responding to signals on fixed industrial trackage.

sources.title: Parallel Systems announces first autonomous rail pilot in Georgia — Railway Technology
sources.claim: Parallel Systems began an FRA-approved commercial pilot of autonomous battery-electric railcars over a 160-mile route on two Georgia short lines linking the Port of Savannah with an inland terminal.

sources.title: Technology update: Locomotive automation — Progressive Railroading
sources.claim: Railspire's Network Controlled Locomotive system, in which the operator selects a route and the system controls throttle and brakes against an authority and speed-limit model, has been deployed on an industrial short line's fleet in its busiest yard; the operator retains situational awareness, so this is supervised rather than unattended operation.
sources.transferJustification: Yard locomotive speed/authority control is the response half of this task; cited as context only, since the human operator still supplies observation.

tasks.label: Inspect engines before and after use to ensure proper operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-shift pre-use inspection of a diesel switcher in a Class I or short-line railroad yard: walk-around of the unit on outdoor yard track (leaks, running gear, wheels, handrails/steps, air hoses, couplers, sand and fuel level), climb into the cab to check gauges, alerter, lights, horn/bell, sanders and wipers, run an air brake application/release test, then complete and sign the daily inspection report / check the FRA blue card. All weather, day or night.

End-of-shift post-use inspection on the servicing or ready track: look the unit over for newly developed defects (fuel/oil/coolant leaks, dragging or broken parts, hot wheels or bearings, damaged safety appliances), check cab for defective equipment, note fuel/sand needs, report defects in writing, secure the locomotive (hand brake, isolate, shut down or leave idling).

Hostler at a diesel service facility / enginehouse: move inbound locomotives over the fuel pad and inspection pit, check engine oil, water and fuel levels, sand, batteries and air system, walk the unit inside the shop and over the pit, tag or write up defects, and release the unit to the ready track for the next crew.

Industrial plant, steel mill, refinery or port terminal plant switcher / trackmobile: pre-shift engine check by the operator — engine oil, coolant, fuel, battery, air compressor and reservoir drains, brakes, lights, horn, couplers and coupler air — on grimy indoor/outdoor plant trackage, followed by a post-shift check and log entry.

Quarry, mine, sand pit or construction-project dinkey / small industrial locomotive: pre- and post-use inspection outdoors on temporary or rough trackage — check fluid levels, fuel, air brakes, running gear, listen to the engine on start-up, look for damage from the day's rough service; older equipment, no fixed layout, mud/dust/weather.

sources.system: Spot ('Spotty') with Energy Robotics inspection software
sources.developer: Boston Dynamics / Energy Robotics for Deutsche Bahn (DB Cargo)
sources.title: Spot the walking robot helps with train maintenance | DB Cargo
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics Spot ('Spotty'), with Energy Robotics software, was trialed at DB Cargo's Mainz freight wagon depot to identify wagons by RFID and perform visual inspection of axles from the maintenance pit; it performs camera/AI-based visual damage detection only, with no manipulation, fluid-level checks or functional tests.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: rail rolling-stock pre-service visual inspection in a depot. It is the closest demonstrated robotic analogue to a locomotive walk-around, but it covers only exterior imaging of wagons — no engine compartment, fluid levels, cab equipment or brake/horn/sander functional tests, and the trial gives no evidence of unattended autonomous operation.

sources.system: Intelligent freight-train inspection robots (underside + side inspection robots)
sources.developer: China Energy Railway Equipment Co., Ltd. (CHN Energy)
sources.title: China introduces robotic inspection of freight trains-Xinhua
sources.claim: A three-robot set (one under-car crawler plus two side robots with articulated arms) inspects freight trains in China Energy Railway Equipment's maintenance depot at Huanghua Port, photographing key areas and flagging 120+ suspected fault types for staff review; it inspects freight cars' exteriors and undersides, not locomotive engines or cabs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: pre-departure mechanical inspection of rail vehicles by car inspectors. It shows machine inspection can replace the visual walk-around portion in a purpose-built depot inspection lane, but freight cars have no prime mover, and the robots do no fluid-level, cab, or functional (brake/light/horn/sander) checks and their findings are reviewed by staff.

sources.title: Automating the Rail Yard with Husky Observer - Clearpath Robotics
sources.claim: Clearpath's Husky Observer autonomous ground robot was deployed at a Class I automotive rail yard in the ... US to run inspection missions — navigating autonomously between tracks and capturing camera/LiDAR data at defined inspection points (e.g., railcar spacing, RFID) — showing autonomous mobility in a working rail yard but not vehicle mechanical inspection.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous inspection rounds in a rail yard. Establishes that a robot can move about the yard environment of this task and take sensor readings, but the demonstrated output is spacing measurement and RFID reading, not a locomotive condition inspection.

sources.developer: Norfolk Southern / Georgia Tech Research Institute
sources.title: Digital Inspection Portal Uses AI and Machine Vision to Examine Moving Trains | GTRI
sources.claim: Norfolk Southern's Digital Train Inspection portals, developed with GTRI, are fixed wayside machine-vision gantries deployed on the NS network that image the top, bottom, sides and ends of passing trains (including locomotives) and flag mechanical defects; they are a sensing installation covering exterior components only and supplement, not replace, human inspections.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated mechanical inspection of rail equipment in motion. Shows the exterior-imaging portion of an inspection can be automated at a purpose-built wayside site, but the portal does not act on the equipment, cannot open compartments, check fluid or sand levels, enter a cab, or run brake and lighting tests.

sources.title: Robotic inspection for railway and transportation | ANYbotics
sources.claim: ANYbotics' ANYmal quadruped is a commercially deployed autonomous inspection robot that runs repeatable routes in industrial plants collecting visual, thermal and acoustic data, reading gauges and detecting leaks or hot components, including in rail-sector infrastructure applications.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous routine condition-monitoring rounds on industrial machinery (gauge reading, thermal and leak checks) — the sensing half of an engine check. It does not demonstrate opening locomotive engine-compartment doors, reading dipsticks or sight glasses, or operating cab controls to test brakes, sanders, lights and horn.

tasks.label: Apply and release hand brakes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Classification/flat switching yard: after shoving a cut of cars to a track, the worker walks the cut on ballast, climbs a ladder or uses a ground-level brake stick, and winds the geared hand brake wheel or ratchet lever on the required number of cars to full chain load (~138 lb applied at the wheel), then verifies each is applied.

Same yard, reverse operation: before a cut is coupled and moved, the worker locates cars with hand brakes applied, releases each wheel/lever (or trips the quick release) from ground or ladder, and verifies the chain is slack so cars are not dragged with brakes set.

Industrial plant, mill, grain elevator, or quarry served by an in-plant switching crew: hand brakes applied on cars spotted at loading/unloading points on grades and released when pulled, on plant-controlled premises with varied car types, outdoors in all weather.

Remote or temporary trackage taken as found — construction-project spur, industry lead with poor footing, storage track in overgrown or unmaintained condition — where the worker walks in, applies or releases hand brakes on cars, with no institution maintaining the site to a standard.

Hostler/engine-terminal work: securing a locomotive or dinkey on a shop or ready track by applying its hand brake (cab-mounted wheel or platform-mounted lever/wheel), and releasing it before moving the unit.

Problem hand brakes: stiff, rusted, frozen, chain kinked or off the sheave, on a car in snow/ice or at night; the worker must apply extra force with a brake stick or climb the car, judge whether the brake is defective, and tag/report it or use an alternative means of securement.

sources.system: Electrically Driven Set and Release Hand Brake (EDHB)
sources.developer: Sharma & Associates, Inc. / Federal Railroad Administration
sources.title: Railroad Freight Car Remote Controlled Electrically Driven Set & Release Hand Brake (EDHB) – Optimization for Increased Reliability and Performance (DOT/FRA/ORD-19/03)
sources.claim: FRA and Sharma & Associates built Electrically Driven Set and Release ... Brake (EDHB) units that retrofit a freight car's geared hand brake and perform the full set and release cycle under closed-loop machine control (torque/application/release feedback) from a single push-button command; three prototypes were field tested on the FAST train at the Transportation ... and passed AAR-defined lab and field performance requirements.

sources.system: Electrically Driven Set and Release Hand Brake (EDHB)
sources.developer: Sharma & Associates, Inc. / Federal Railroad Administration
sources.title: DOT/FRA/ORD-19/03 EDHB Optimization for Increased Reliability and Performance
sources.claim: The same report states the mechanical requirement the machine must meet (the chain load a person normally produces by cranking) and that three prototype units were field ... on the FAST train at TTC after review by the AAR Geared Hand Brake Mechanical Engineering Committee's Remote Operation Hand Brake task force.

sources.system: Wireless Train Network + electronically deployed hand brakes (Advanced Devices Train & Test Bed)
sources.title: U.S. Department of Transportation Federal Railroad Administration (Research Results / ADT&TB report)
sources.claim: FRA's Advanced Devices Train & Test Bed carried a wireless train network demonstration built to activate and deactivate the Sharma & Associates electronically deployed hand brakes, extending machine set/release of car hand brakes to command from the locomotive in a revenue-service-like test environment.

sources.system: Autonomous brake bleeding robot (GE Global Research / Carnegie Mellon)
sources.developer: GE Global Research with Carnegie Mellon University
sources.title: An Integrated Robotic System for Autonomous Brake Bleeding in Rail Yards
sources.claim: A mobile manipulator (Clearpath Grizzly base with a Motoman SIA20F arm) autonomously located and actuated railcar air-brake bleed levers in a hump yard; this is the closest demonstrated autonomous manipulation of brake apparatus on unmodified cars in a working yard, but it is a single lever pull, not winding a geared hand brake to ~138 lb chain load, and it remained a research prototype.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: actuating a railcar brake device in a yard. It substantiates autonomous outdoor navigation and single-lever actuation on standard cars, but not hand brake application, which needs many turns of a wheel at high torque and often work at height; cited here to show why E2 is not reached.

sources.system: Fiberglass brake stick (manual hand tool, non-robotic)
sources.developer: Union Pacific with an industry vendor
sources.title: Practical Teamwork, Real Impact: Union Pacific's Safer Way to Set Hand Brakes
sources.claim: State of practice on the largest US freight railroad as of March 2026 is manual: crews set and release hand brakes by hand from the ground with fiberglass brake sticks, of which more than 11,000 have been bought since 2023; no robotic system performs this work in the yard.
sources.transferJustification: Negative/context evidence for the same task: shows that in 2026 hand brake application and release in US yards is performed by workers with hand tools, with no fielded robotic substitute.

tasks.label: Signal crew members for movement of engines or trains, using lanterns, hand signals, radios, or telephones.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Confer with conductors and other workers via radiotelephones or computers to exchange switching information.

tasks.label: Inspect track for defects such as broken rails and switch malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Class I or short-line flat switching yard: while shoving and pulling cuts of cars, the engineer/hostler watches the track and switches ahead from the cab and reports misaligned or unlocked switch points, obstructions, derails left in place, and visibly broken or kinked rail on yard leads and body tracks; day and night, all weather.

Scheduled inspection sweep of yard, lead and spur tracks (on foot or from a slow-moving engine/hi-rail): looking for broken rails and cracked joint bars, missing bolts and spikes, wide gauge, pumping/fouled ballast and rail gaps; defects documented and reported to the maintenance-of-way department.

Hands-on switch/derail check: walk to a hand-throw switch, operate the lever, verify the points fit tight against the stock rail and that the target and lock work, clear ballast, debris, snow or ice from the point area, and report a malfunctioning switch or damaged switch rod.

In-plant or terminal trackage at a steel mill, chemical plant, grain facility, port or intermodal terminal: embedded rail in pavement, spilled product/scrap fouling the rail, damaged grade crossings, worn frogs and derails; the hostler-engineer inspects the track before moving equipment over it.

Quarry, mine or construction-project dinkey track: portable or temporary track laid on rough grade, mud, washouts and shifting layouts; the operator inspects for broken rail, spread gauge, undermined or floating ties and misaligned joints before hauling loads.

sources.system: CSX autonomous drone inspection (DJI Matrice 350 RTK + Phase One IXM 100, Hextronics Atlas dock, FlytBase autonomy, CASIA G detect-and-avoid)
sources.title: How CSX Transportation is Mitigating Rail Risks using Autonomous Drone Ops in US
sources.claim: CSX operates docked, autonomously flown inspection drones at 13 rail-yard sites that fly preprogrammed missions over tracks and run edge machine-learning models to detect switch-point gaps >1/8 in, joint-bar defects, rail gaps >2 in and gauge problems, reporting defect locations to maintenance crews.

sources.system: CSX autonomous yard drone inspection program
sources.title: 'Force Multipliers' - Railway Age
sources.claim: Trade-press corroboration that CSX's yard drone fleet measures track gauge, identifies broken rail and detects switch-point gaps greater than 1/8 inch, with FAA BVLOS approval (February 2025) for autonomous drone operation at those yards, missions triggered from the yard office and streamed to a remote command center.

sources.system: Alstom ATO GoA4 shunting locomotive with obstacle detection system (Lineas locomotive, ProRail infrastructure)
sources.title: GoA4 shunting locomotive demonstration
sources.claim: A GoA4 fully autonomous shunting locomotive detected and correctly reacted to an incorrectly positioned switch and other obstacles in a yard setting near Breda with no staff aboard, demonstrating machine detection of switch misalignment ahead of a moving locomotive.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is autonomous shunting movement; the perception it exercises - recognising an incorrectly positioned switch and obstructions on the track ahead from a moving locomotive - is the same detection the yard engineer performs when inspecting for switch malfunctions while switching.

sources.system: BNSF unmanned geometry ('geo') cars / ENSCO-type autonomous track inspection systems
sources.title: Geo car technologies detect what the eye can't | Rail Talk | BNSF
sources.claim: BNSF runs unmanned (crewless) track inspection car sets using ultrasound, radar and machine vision to find rail and tie defects, operating around the clock with remote analysts and covering up to 400,000 track miles a year.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is mainline automated track inspection; it finds the same defect classes (broken or internally flawed rail, wide gauge, defective ties and joints) on the same asset, so the sensing and defect-calling transfer to yard and industrial trackage.

sources.system: Automated Track Inspection (ATI) programs using autonomous geometry inspection vehicles
sources.developer: BNSF Railway / AAR member railroads (ENSCO, Holland, MERMEC systems)
sources.title: AAR seeks FRA permission to scale back visual track inspections where automated systems are used to find defects - Trains
sources.claim: Regulatory record showing autonomous track inspection matches or exceeds human visual inspection in defect finding: in BNSF's FRA pilot, automated systems found 200 track geometry ... found by visual inspection, and FRA waivers permitted reduced visual inspection frequency on those territories.
sources.transferJustification: Quality benchmark for the same task - finding track defects - performed by autonomous inspection platforms in place of a human inspector.

tasks.label: Observe water levels and oil, air, and steam pressure gauges to ensure proper operation of equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Couple and uncouple air hoses and electrical connections between cars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Flat switching in a Class I terminal or classification freight yard: after a joint is made, the worker steps in between two freight cars standing on ballast, lifts the two hanging brake-pipe hoses, mates the glad hands, and opens both angle cocks; reverses the sequence (close cock, part the hoses) before cutting away. Mixed car types (hoppers, tanks, boxcars, autoracks), varying hose lengths and wear, day and night, all weather.

Industrial plant, quarry, mine or terminal spur worked by a dinkey/plant switcher or railcar mover: the operator couples the mover or locomotive to a cut of cars at a loading spot, connects the mover's air hose to the first car's glad hand and opens the angle cock, then disconnects after the cars are spotted. In-plant trackage with debris, spilled material, narrow clearances, sometimes on grade.

Hostler work at an engine terminal / servicing track: making up or breaking up a locomotive consist — plugging and unplugging the 27-pin MU jumper cable and connecting/disconnecting several air hoses (brake pipe, main reservoir, actuating, independent) between units, stowing cables and hoses in dummy receptacles.

Transit / EMU / metro yard: coupling and uncoupling units of multiple-unit equipment whose automatic couplers carry the pneumatic and electrical connections; the operator drives units together and completes or releases the connections from the cab.
Conventional locomotive-hauled passenger coach yard: connecting and disconnecting glad-hand air hoses plus heavy HEP/communication jumper cables between coaches or between locomotive and first coach.

Degraded conditions in any of the above settings: hoses frozen or ice-caked, twisted, dragging or damaged; blown gasket or torn hose that must be swapped out; mismatched coupler heights, cars standing on a curve or over a grade crossing; mud, snow, darkness.

tasks.label: Drive engines within railroad yards or other establishments to couple, uncouple, or switch railroad cars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Class I / large railroad classification or flat-switching yard: yard engineer (often a remote-control operator) pulls and shoves cuts of 10-70 mixed freight cars over many tracks to break down inbound trains and build outbound ones, coupling at controlled speed to a ground crew's radio/hand signals, working around hand-thrown and powered switches, other crews, foreign cars of unknown condition, at night and in all weather.

Hostler at a locomotive servicing facility / engine terminal: moves locomotives (running and dead-in-tow) between arrival tracks, fuel and sand racks, wash and shop tracks, turntables and ready tracks; couples units into outbound consists and spots them precisely at servicing stands, with mechanical forces working on the ground under blue-flag protection.

In-plant switching at an industrial establishment (steel mill, auto plant, refinery/chemical works, grain elevator, paper mill, transload or port terminal): drives a plant switcher or trackmobile on private track to pull loaded cars from unloaders and spot empties at doors, scales and dumpers, on a fixed internal track network controlled by the plant.

Short line / terminal railroad local switching off railroad property: takes cuts of cars from the yard out to customer spurs and team tracks, works street trackage and public grade crossings, opens gates and derails, and spots cars on varied, sometimes poorly maintained industry track at sites the railroad does not control.

Dinkey / narrow-gauge or industrial locomotive at a quarry, mine or construction project: hauls material cars between pit/face, crusher, stockpile or port dock on a dedicated haul rail line, coupling and uncoupling cars and spotting them at loaders and dumping points, often underground or on rough, dusty ground.

instances.label: Class I flat/hump yard: yard engineer/hostler walks or rides alongside a cut of freight cars during switching, visually inspecting couplers/knuckles, air hoses and glad hands, brake rigging and shoes, hand brakes, wheels, doors/hatches, shifted or leaking lading; outdoors on ballast, day or night, all weather, mixed car types.

Receiving/departure track: condition check of an assembled outbound or arriving train (often 100+ cars) before movement - spotting bad-order cars, dragging or missing parts, defective couplers/hoses - and reporting defects to the yardmaster/mechanical desk; standard yard tracks with lighting, in coordination with carmen.

Engine terminal service track or enginehouse: hostler inspects locomotives before or after moving them - leaks, damaged running gear, fuel/oil/water sight gauges, sand level, air hoses, handrails/steps, lights, cab condition and defect card; indoor bay or outdoor service track.

Industrial plant, steel mill, grain/chemical terminal or port: dinkey/plant switcher operator inspects cars spotted at loading and unloading points - hatches and doors closed and secured, chocks and derails, product leaks, load condition, hand brakes and couplers; congested plant trackage controlled by the plant.

Quarry, mine, or construction-project trackage: operator inspects the dinkey locomotive and work cars on unimproved, muddy or dusty track taken as found, with no fixed layout, temporary spurs and site equipment mixed in.

tasks.label: Spot cars for loading and unloading at customer locations.

instances.label: Short line / terminal-railroad local crew spotting cars at assorted customers along a branch (lumber yard, plastics plant, scrapyard, warehouse dock): run out from the yard, line hand-throw switches and derails, shove cuts over public grade crossings on weed-grown industry track, cut air, uncouple, place each car on a chalk/door mark, tie handbrakes, pull the empties.

In-plant switching at a large industrial facility (refinery, chemical plant, steel mill, auto assembly plant): plant switch engine or railcar mover pulls tank cars/gondolas/boxcars from the plant's receiving track and spots them at loading racks, unloading pits and dock doors to a marked spot, under blue-flag protection and with plant loading personnel present.

Bulk loadout/unload spotting at a mine, quarry, grain elevator or coal facility: place a cut of hoppers on the dedicated loadout track and advance them car by car under the loading spout (or over the unloading pit) at creep speed until each car is loaded/emptied, then pull the loaded string clear.

Captive shuttle service on a private industrial railway: same fixed set of cars cycled repeatedly between a mine/plant loading point and a dock, dumper or receiving hopper a few miles away, spotting the cars at the loader and at the dump pockets each cycle.

Transload/port terminal spotting: move cars between a storage yard and transload pads, warehouse dome doors or unloading pits inside the terminal, matching many different car types and commodities to trucks and forklifts on a shifting daily order list.

tasks.label: Operate track switches, derails, automatic switches, and retarders to change routing of train or cars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Flat switching yard: a yard crew member on the ground lines hand-throw switch stands on yard ladders and leads to route cuts of cars into the correct classification track during a switching move, unlocking/relocking, verifying that the points fit tight, in all weather (snow, ice, mud, darkness) with other equipment moving nearby.

Yard/terminal with power-operated (dual-control) switches and interlockings: routes are changed for arriving/departing trains and light locomotives by operating power switches from a control panel, tower, or radio, with point detection and signal indication confirming the route before the movement passes.

Hump yard: operating automatic switches and master/group/tangent retarders that route each cut from the crest to its assigned bowl track and control coupling speed, working from the hump tower console with the hump list, in a high-volume classification yard.

Engine terminal / hostler work: lining switches and setting or releasing derails around shop tracks, ready tracks, wash and fuel pads so locomotives can be moved between service points, including blue-flag protection of tracks where mechanical forces are working.

Industrial plant, port or short-line trackage: a plant switcher or dinkey operator lines in-plant switches and fixed (hinged/sliding) derails to route cars to loading, dumping or weighing spots, on track owned and maintained by the facility, sometimes among plant traffic and loading equipment.

Construction project or quarry temporary trackage: lining hand switches and placing/removing portable derails on track that is relaid as the work advances, with no signaling, uneven ballast, mud and debris, and a layout that differs day to day and site to site.

tasks.label: Perform routine repair and maintenance duties.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Refuel a locomotive or dinkey: spot the unit at the fuel stand (or meet a fuel truck), open the fill cap, couple the fuel nozzle, fill to automatic shutoff, decouple and stow the hose, wipe drips, log gallons. Outdoor service track at an engine terminal, plant or quarry, in all weather.

Full service-track servicing of a locomotive consist: fill the sand boxes from the sand tower while standing on the deck, add lube oil and engine coolant, top off water, drain/flush the toilet, restock cab supplies, clean the windshield and headlight glass, and note defects. Outdoor service track/fuel pad under a canopy.

Minor running repairs and component change-outs in the yard or enginehouse: replace burst air hoses and gladhands, coupler knuckles, brake shoes, headlight lamps and wipers, blown fuses or tripped breakers; tighten leaking fittings; free stuck hand brakes. Done on ballast, reaching under and around the unit, with hand tools, in heat, cold, rain or snow.

Housekeeping and cleaning of the unit: climb into the cab, remove trash and leftover crew supplies, sweep and mop the cab floor, wipe the control stand, windows and mirrors, clean walkways, steps and handrails, wipe up oil and fuel, dispose of oily rags.

Upkeep of a dinkey or small industrial locomotive at a quarry, mill or construction project: grease fittings and rod pins, check engine oil, coolant and hydraulic levels, blow out or change air filters, check the battery, replace worn hoses or belts. Usually done outdoors at the work site with no shop, layout differing site to site.

Ancillary maintenance around the yard and servicing area: lubricate switch points and derails, clear snow, ice, mud and debris from switches and walkways, clean up spilled sand or fuel, replace lamps and markers, restock tools and supplies.

sources.title: Scott | Autonomous Truck Refueling - The Robot Revolution
sources.claim: Scott Automation's ROBOFUEL uses a vision-guided ABB/KUKA robot arm housed in a container to autonomously locate a heavy diesel vehicle's fuel receiver, open the cap, couple the nozzle and fill the tank; Roy Hill mine has run an in-pit robotic refuelling device since 2016.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous refuelling of mining haul trucks. Transfers to locomotive/dinkey fuelling: the same operation sequence (locate a fill port on a large diesel vehicle parked at a fuel stand, open the cap, couple a high-flow nozzle, fill to shutoff, decouple) on comparably sized outdoor industrial equipment, with vision handling parking-position variation.

sources.title: Autonomous refuelling solution for mining trucks from Universal Field Robots - International Mining
sources.claim: ROBOFUEL is in commercial service at multiple mine sites, including refuelling an autonomous Komatsu 930E haul-truck fleet in the Pilbara, i.e. routine unattended fuelling of heavy diesel equipment.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: fuelling large diesel rail/mining equipment at a fixed fuelling point is the closest demonstrated analogue to a hostler fuelling a locomotive at the service track.

sources.system: Autonomous rollingstock cleaning robots (floor and surface robots)
sources.title: Downer develops the world's first fully autonomous rollingstock cleaning robots
sources.claim: Downer and Deakin University built two autonomous rolling-stock cleaning robots (a floor scrubber and a 6-DOF surface-cleaning manipulator for seats and windows) and trialled them on Downer-maintained passenger fleets; the work is a proof-of-concept working alongside cleaning staff, aimed at passenger saloons rather than locomotive cabs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: interior cleaning of rail vehicles. It is the nearest analogue to cab housekeeping, but the demonstrated setting is a level, open passenger saloon entered at platform level, not a cluttered locomotive cab reached by a vertical ladder, and no trash pick-up or oil wipe-down is shown.

sources.title: ANYbotics and Stadler Service AG Explore the Future of Train Maintenance
sources.claim: ANYbotics' ANYmal quadruped has been used with Stadler Service to run autonomous inspection missions on rolling stock inside maintenance depots; the collaboration covers data collection and inspection only, not physical repair or servicing actions.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to show the frontier of depot/yard robotics for rolling stock is autonomous sensing and data capture; no manipulation of worn parts, fasteners or consumables is demonstrated, so it cannot substantiate repair instances.

sources.title: AI and robotics are transforming freight trains in Pittsburgh - Axios Pittsburgh
sources.claim: Wabtec's Rail Ghost is a camera-equipped robotic sled that slides beneath standing railcars to inspect brakes, couplings and other undercarriage items without removing cars from the track; it was shown as a prototype/model, and it performs inspection only.
sources.transferJustification: Cited as the state of rail-yard robotics for undercarriage work: it inspects but does not replace brake shoes, hoses or knuckles, so it does not substantiate the repair instances.

tasks.label: Drive locomotives to and from various stations in roundhouses to have locomotives cleaned, serviced, repaired, or supplied.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Class I / large freight railroad diesel servicing facility: hostler takes an inbound road locomotive consist (1-3 units, already coupled) off the arrival track and runs it down the service track, spotting precisely at the fuel/sand/water pad, then moves it to the ready track. Low speed, ground servicemen present, radio coordination, yard switches, blue-flag protection.

Moving a self-powered locomotive into and later out of the enginehouse/back-shop bay for scheduled repair: slow entry through shop doors onto a shop track, precise spotting over a drop pit or jacks inside the building, brakes secured, then removal to the ready track after work is complete.
Handling a dead or disabled locomotive: coupling a live unit to it, dragging it from the arrival track to the shop or a dead line, uncoupling, and securing it with hand brakes and chocks.

Passenger/commuter maintenance facility (Amtrak, commuter authority): hostler moves locomotives and cab-car consists among arrival tracks, the wash rack, the fuel/water station, and the service-and-inspection building, at creep speed with cleaners and inspectors working nearby.

Industrial plant, mine or quarry: plant switcher or dinkey is run at end of shift from the working trackage to its fueling point and maintenance shed inside the plant-controlled site; single small locomotive, short private trackage, plant traffic and personnel around.

Short line, heritage or tourist railroad roundhouse: moving a steam or vintage diesel locomotive to the ash pit, coal/water spouts, turntable and stall; manual turntable alignment, non-standard aging controls, ad hoc track condition.

sources.system: Škoda Group 'Smart Depot' autonomous tram (Škoda 36T at RNV Möhlstraße depot)
sources.title: Autonomous tram operations demonstrated in Mannheim - Railway Gazette International
sources.claim: Škoda 36T trams move autonomously inside RNV's Möhlstraße depot in Mannheim, performing shunting, stabling, precise stopping and passage through the washing plant — the direct analog of hostling rail vehicles between servicing stations in a depot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: driverless movement of rail vehicles within a maintenance depot to servicing positions. Same object class (rail vehicle on fixed track), same environment (depot/servicing facility), same precision requirement (spotting at a wash/service position), which is what a hostler does with locomotives.

sources.system: Škoda Group Smart Depot autonomous tram operation
sources.title: Automatization and digitalization: Škoda's approach to smart depots and intelligent urban mobility - presented in Mannheim
sources.claim: The same Mannheim depot demonstration covered automatic parking, routing between depot tracks, obstacle handling and automated passage ... the washing facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: moving rail vehicles to a wash plant and stabling road inside a servicing facility, which is the hostler's movement to cleaning/servicing stations; obstacle handling covers the ground staff and equipment found on service tracks.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: driverless operation of a full-size shunting locomotive inside a working marshalling yard — the same machine and the same class of low-speed, staffed-yard movement that a hostler performs on engine service tracks.
