sources.claim: China's first freight-car intelligent inspection robot group (an under-car robot plus a trackless side robot) entered use in 2025 on a railway servicing line, performing the train technical inspection previously done by car inspectors, identifying 120+ fault types with >98% accuracy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic pre-departure technical inspection of rail equipment on a servicing line): shows robots performing the inspecting-and-reporting role of a rail yard worker, but on wheels/brake components rather than fuel, water and sand supplies.

tasks.label: Climb ladders to tops of cars to set brakes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Flat/classification yard: after a switching move, the brakeman walks a cut of freight cars standing on a yard track, climbs the end ladder of one or more cars, and winds the hand-brake wheel down until the chain is tight and the brake is fully applied, then verifies it. Mixed car types, day or night, all weather, loose ballast between tracks.

Railroad-controlled mechanical facility (repair track, car shop, locomotive servicing or storage track): hand brakes set on cars spotted for repair, storage or blue-flag protection. Paved or graded walkways, lighting, controlled access, cars spotted at known locations.

Older or high-bodied cars in a yard where the brake wheel is high on the car end or at roof level (older boxcars, high covered hoppers, some tank cars): a full ladder climb and an awkward, high-force reach to wind a stiff or rusted brake wheel with slack chain.

Industry track at a customer facility (grain elevator, chemical plant, mine loadout, team track): cars spotted for loading/unloading must be secured with hand brakes. Layout differs from customer to customer, footing is mud, weeds, gravel or spilled product, and the customer's own vehicles and equipment are present.

Road/mainline service: securing a train or cut of cars on a grade, at a remote siding, or after an emergency or mechanical stop. Ballast footing, embankments, night, rain/snow/ice, cars anywhere along a long train, no fixed infrastructure.

sources.title: An Integrated Robotic System for Autonomous Brake Bleeding in Rail Yards
sources.claim: An integrated autonomous mobile manipulator located railcars, detected the brake bleed lever on each car and physically actuated it, field tested on randomly selected cars in a fully operational classification yard, day and night.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: releasing (bleeding) a railcar air brake rather than winding its hand brake. Transfer is partial - the same object class (brake actuation hardware on standing freight cars) is perceived and forcefully actuated autonomously by a robot arm - but hand braking additionally needs a climb and many turns against rising torque, so the transfer holds only where the brake wheel is presented to the machine in a known pose (E1).

sources.title: (PDF) An Integrated Robotic System for Autonomous Brake Bleeding in Rail Yards
sources.claim: The same system autonomously navigated along a line of railcars, detected the brake lever on each car, positioned itself and computed and executed the actuation trajectory.
sources.transferJustification: Same related-task transfer as the previous item: autonomous machine perception and powered actuation of freight-car brake hardware; it does not include climbing to a car-top brake wheel or applying multi-turn hand-brake torque.

sources.system: Electrically Driven Set & Release Hand Brake (EDHB)
sources.developer: Sharma & Associates, Inc. for the Federal Railroad Administration
sources.title: Railroad Freight Car Remote Controlled Electrically Driven Set & Release Hand Brake (EDHB) - Wireless Control Development
sources.claim: Prototype motor-driven hand brakes for freight cars apply and release the car's hand brake on a remote command, removing the need for a person ... climb the car; developed and tested under FRA research contract, prototype stage only.
sources.transferJustification: Same end output (a freight-car hand brake applied to the required force) achieved by a powered mechanism executing automatically after a single command rather than by a person climbing a ladder. It is a car-mounted actuator at prototype stage, so it shows the mechanical application problem is solved but not that a free-standing robot performs the job in a yard.

sources.system: Motoman/Yaskawa robotic welding system for rail wagon manufacture
sources.developer: Yaskawa (Motoman) system integrated for Rio Tinto wagon production
sources.title: Robots to Rail - AMTIL
sources.claim: Industrial robot cells perform forceful, precise work on fixtured rail-wagon structures in a purpose-built manufacturing setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic welding of rail wagons rather than brake setting. It substantiates only the environment premise for E1 - that railcar-scale workpieces are routinely brought to fixtured robot cells where machines apply accurate, forceful operations to them.

sources.title: Amazon FAR's Ladderman: Unitree Robots Climb Ladders
sources.claim: A humanoid learned to climb ladders autonomously, but the manipulation work performed at the top of the ladder in the demonstration was teleoperated.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: ladder climbing plus light manipulation at height in a lab. Cited to show the state of the art on the climb-and-work combination; because the at-height manipulation was teleoperated and the objects trivial compared with a stiff hand-brake wheel, it cannot support completion of this task in a yard or in the field.

sources.title: Vertical ladder climbing by the HRP-2 humanoid robot
sources.claim: A humanoid robot was shown to have the actuation capability to climb vertical industrial-standard ladders using an offline contact plan in laboratory trials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: vertical ladder climbing only, in a laboratory with pre-planned contacts and no work performed at the top; cited to bound the state of the art, not to support completion.

tasks.label: Set flares, flags, lanterns, or torpedoes in front and at rear of trains during emergency stops to warn oncoming trains.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Rear-end flag protection after an unplanned stop on main track in road territory, daylight and fair weather: the brakeman/conductor detrains, walks back the prescribed distance (often a mile or more) along ballast shoulder, ditches, curves and grade crossings, drops lighted fusees, places torpedoes on the rail head, and displays a red flag until relieved.

Same rear-end protection performed at night or in adverse weather (rain, snow, fog, ice, cold), carrying a lighted lantern and fusee case, judging sight distance on curves and in cuts, planting/lighting fusees in ballast in the dark.

Head-end or adjacent-track protection after an emergency stop (broken knuckle, derailment, obstruction, dragging equipment): crew member goes ahead of the locomotive or to the adjacent main track and sets a lighted fusee/flag quickly, under time pressure, close to the train.

Fusee relay protection: dropping single lighted fusees off the rear at intervals not exceeding the burning time while the train stands or moves at restricted speed, to protect against a following train on the same track.

Protection of a stopped train or cut of cars in a rail yard, terminal, or at an industry track: setting flags, lanterns, or fusees on flat, lighted, institution-controlled premises with standard track layout and controlled access.

Recovery of protection: after the emergency is cleared, extinguishing and retrieving unburned fusees, removing torpedoes from the railhead, taking down flags/lanterns, walking back and restowing the flagging kit on the locomotive before the train departs.

sources.title: FANUC Robots Automate Precise Automotive Process | Case Study
sources.claim: Deployed FANUC M-20iD/25 industrial robots in four fenced robotic cells autonomously feed, insert and place/weld small plastic clips with ±0.02 mm repeatability at production reliability — i.e., grasping a small hand-sized device from a presented magazine and setting it precisely at a fixtured position is routine, commercially deployed E1 capability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated feeding, insertion and precise placement of small parts in a fenced cell. Under the E1 counterfactual the fusee/lantern/flag and its placement point are presented fixtured, so the residual physical act is grasp-transport-place-actuate of a hand-sized object at a known position, matching this cell's object size, precision and reliability.

sources.developer: Creare (US DOT-sponsored) with Dartmouth ENGS 89/90 team
sources.title: Development of an Automated Marker Deployment Mechanism for Autonomous Trucks
sources.claim: As of a DOT-sponsored program, automated vehicles had no ability to deploy the required roadside warning triangles/flares behind a stopped vehicle; Creare is developing a prototype rover for the purpose, and even a triangle was judged unwieldy for a robot to deploy.
sources.transferJustification: Directly analogous task: placing physical warning devices at prescribed distances behind a stopped vehicle to warn oncoming traffic in an unstructured outdoor corridor. It shows the capability does not exist beyond prototype stage, supporting negative judgments at E2/E3.

sources.system: Waymo Driver and Aurora Driver autonomous trucks
sources.title: Regulators deny roadside warning exemption for autonomous trucks
sources.claim: The two leading US autonomous trucking developers sought regulatory relief from placing physical roadside warning devices, proposing cab-mounted beacons instead, and FMCSA rejected the request — evidence that commercially deployed autonomous road vehicles cannot place warning devices behind a stopped vehicle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: deploying warning devices in front of and behind a stopped vehicle on a transport right-of-way. The most capable fielded autonomous vehicles avoid the manipulation entirely, indicating no system performs this device placement in unstructured corridors.

sources.title: An Integrated Robotic System for Autonomous Brake Bleeding in Rail Yards
sources.claim: A mobile manipulator (Clearpath Grizzly base with Motoman SIA20F arm) autonomously detected and manipulated railcar brake levers during field tests in an operational hump yard, day and night — the closest rail-yard outdoor autonomous manipulation, but a research prototype for a different, fixed-on-the-car manipulation task.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous outdoor manipulation on railcars inside a rail yard (E2). It bounds the state of the art: a research prototype acting on a fixed lever on a car, not travelling the track to set, ignite and later retrieve pyrotechnic warning devices, so it cannot substantiate this task at E2.

sources.title: CivDot | Construction Robot for Automated layout – Measur Drones
sources.claim: The leading commercially deployed autonomous outdoor layout robot marks prescribed coordinates with spray paint only; human crews still follow it to install the physical markers (flags, nails, stakes).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomously travelling outdoor terrain to prescribed points and leaving a marker. Even this commercial system stops short of placing a physical device, so it does not substantiate setting flags/fusees along a right-of-way at E3.

sources.title: RATP: Inspections after dark | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Spot quadrupeds are deployed by a rail operator to run autonomous inspection missions in metro infrastructure, but the deployment is sensing/inspection only — no placement or activation of warning devices.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous legged mobility on rail infrastructure inside an institution-controlled facility. It shows fielded rail-sector robots do inspection, not the mobile manipulation of pyrotechnic warning devices this task requires, supporting negative E2/E3 judgments.

tasks.label: Refuel and lubricate engines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fuel-only stop at a Class I railroad fuel pad / service track: a locomotive consist is spotted at the rack, the servicer couples the heavy high-flow fast-fill nozzle to the tank receiver on the side of the fuel tank, dispenses several thousand gallons to automatic shut-off, stows the hose and records gallons. Outdoor paved fueling facility controlled by the railroad, day or night, all weather.

Full fluid service at the same fuel pad: fuel the unit, then check the engine lube-oil sight glass/dipstick in the engine compartment and pump engine oil into the crankcase fill from a lube reel until the correct level, top up coolant, and check for leaks before releasing the unit.

Mobile fuel-truck servicing of locomotives standing on yard tracks: the servicer drives the fuel/lube truck along the yard road, positions alongside the unit, drags the fuel hose across ballast between tracks, fuels the tank, adds engine oil and water from the truck's reels, in rain, snow, mud and darkness, with switching movements nearby.

Mobile fueling away from the yard: locomotive or work-train power tied down at an industry siding, branch line, or maintenance-of-way location; fuel truck parks on a grade crossing or dirt access road, hoses are hand-carried to the unit over uneven ground, fuel and lube oil added with no fixed facilities present.

Engine-house / shop fluid service on a unit standing over a service pit: adding lube oil to the crankcase from a shop hose reel up to the sight-glass mark, topping the cooling system, and refilling the air-compressor lubricator, working inside the locomotive engine room and on the walkways.

Grease and oil-can lubrication rounds before release: pumping grease into fittings on running gear, brake rigging, hand-brake chain and compressor, and on heritage/steam power 'oiling around' - filling oil cups and rod bearings by hand with a long-spout can, crawling under and around the machine.

sources.title: SCOTT making ROBOFUEL refuelling system progress with AHS mining truck fleets - International Mining
sources.claim: Scott Automation's ROBOFUEL autonomously refuels large diesel mining trucks at an unmanned refuelling station on an iron-ore mine site; the first autonomous-truck installation reached site acceptance in late 2019 ... runs in production.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: refuelling a heavy off-highway diesel vehicle. It transfers to locomotive fuelling because the object class (a multi-thousand-litre diesel tank fitted with a commercial fast-fill nozzle/receiver), the coupling precision, the high-flow automatic shut-off procedure and the outdoor industrial servicing bay are the same as at a railroad fuel pad.

sources.title: Robotic refuelling for mines - Robofuel | Scott
sources.claim: ROBOFUEL is a commercial product that uses vision sensing to locate the position and ... parked truck's fuel tank, couples commercial fuel nozzles and receivers ... vehicle modification, and operates in hot, dusty, cold and wet outdoor conditions with drive-off detection.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: the robot handles an unfixtured, driver-parked heavy vehicle in an outdoor industrial fuelling bay, which matches how a locomotive is spotted at a service-track fuel rack.

sources.title: Fast fuel system - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Locomotives are among the vehicle classes fitted with fast fuel systems - the same automatic shut-off nozzle, receiver and level-control hardware used on mining and earthmoving equipment - with ground-level fill points.
sources.transferJustification: Not a robot demonstration; cited only to establish that the fuel-fill interface on railroad locomotives is the same commercial fast-fill nozzle/receiver that ROBOFUEL is built to couple, which is what makes the mining-truck refuelling evidence transfer.

sources.system: Robotic vision-guided oil filling cell (AA9 servo dispenser)
sources.title: Oil Filling Assembly | An Automated System Solution for Generator Engines - GP Reeves
sources.claim: GP Reeves built a production oil-filling cell in which a 6-axis robot with a vision system identifies each engine arriving unfixtured on a conveyor, locates its oil fill port(s) and dispenses the exact crankcase charge to +/-1% in under 70 seconds.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: charging a diesel/gas engine crankcase with lubricating oil. It transfers to the 'lubricate engines' half because the fluid, the fill-port docking action and the volume accuracy required are the same; the difference is that the engine is presented to the machine on a line, i.e. an E1 presentation.

sources.title: Duerr Automated Filling Stations - Duerr
sources.claim: Duerr supplies fully automatic filling stations integrated into vehicle final-assembly lines, including fuel filling equipment for explosion-proof areas that removes manual fuelling work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: filling a vehicle's fuel tank on an assembly line. Transfers to the refuelling half of this task at a fixtured purpose-built station: same fluid, same docking-to-a-fill-port action, hazardous-area rated.

sources.title: Duerr Compact Filling Stations - Duerr
sources.claim: Duerr's BlueStart compact filling system automatically fills the full range of vehicle service fluids, including motor and gearbox oil and coolant, at assembly stations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-controlled dosing of engine oil and coolant into a vehicle at a fixed station; transfers to the oil/coolant top-off portion of locomotive servicing when the unit is presented to the machine.

tasks.label: Start diesel engines to warm engines before runs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine terminal/yard start: a road or yard locomotive has been shut down on a ready or departure track at a Class I yard between assignments; before the run the hostler/firer boards the cab, starts the prime mover, and lets it warm up, build main-reservoir air and charge batteries. Mild-to-moderate weather, standard modern EMD/GE units.

Cold-weather warm cycles: sub-freezing outdoor yard/servicing tracks; the engine must be started (or repeatedly restarted) to keep coolant and lube oil above freezing/operating thresholds and keep the unit ready for its run, sometimes for days of layover.

Outlying/remote layover: a unit parked overnight at a customer's industrial siding, a branch-line siding, or an away-from-home outpost with no servicing facilities or shore power; the crew starts the engine to warm it before the run, working in weather with the site as found.

Short line, industrial, or tourist operation with older non-microprocessor units: the worker starts an aging GP/SW-type locomotive at a small yard or enginehouse (fuel prime, engine start, monitor water temperature during warm-up) before the day's run.

First start after shop work or long dead storage: the unit is stone cold with an isolated/locked-out engine, blue-flag protection to be cleared, drained or weak batteries needing a jump from another unit, and fluid levels to be verified before the engine is primed, started and warmed at the enginehouse/servicing facility.

sources.system: ZTR SmartStart AESS (SmartStart IIe / NexSys III-i)
sources.date: 2026 (product page, retrieved 2026-07); product line in service 30+ years
sources.title: SmartStart: Trusted AESS for Fuel Savings & Emissions Reduction — ZTR
sources.claim: ZTR's SmartStart AESS is an onboard system installed on 10,000+ locomotives that automatically shuts down and restarts the locomotive's diesel prime mover based on engine water and ambient temperature, battery voltage and air pressure, with no manual intervention — i.e., it performs the engine start that keeps the unit warm and ready.

sources.title: SmartStart: Trusted AESS for Fuel Savings & Emissions Reduction — ZTR
sources.claim: SmartStart is retrofittable across locomotive models and vintages, so older non-microprocessor units at short lines and industrial operations can be equipped with the same automatic start capability.

sources.system: Automatic Engine Stop/Start (AESS) on BNSF locomotive fleet
sources.title: Protecting Our Planet — BNSF Sustainability
sources.claim: BNSF reports that AESS automatically restarts idled locomotives when needed for power or for engine health, and that more than 99% of its active locomotive fleet is AESS-equipped — evidence that the automatic engine start is accepted in place of a worker starting the unit across a US Class I fleet in its yards and terminals.

sources.system: Automatic engine stop/start systems mandated under 40 CFR 1033.115(g)
sources.date: Rule 2008, amended through 2023; current eCFR text retrieved 2026-07
sources.title: eCFR :: 40 CFR Part 1033 Subpart B — Emission Standards and Related Requirements
sources.claim: EPA regulation requires all new locomotives to be equipped with automatic engine ... systems that may restart the engine to prevent damage such as coolant freezing or to maintain air pressure and battery charge — the regulatory basis for fleet-wide automatic warm-up starts in US service.

sources.title: HOTSTART APU Features Tier 4 Final Engine and New Cab Heat Option
sources.claim: The HOTSTART locomotive APU is a self-contained auxiliary diesel that automatically starts while the locomotive is shut ... to hold coolant and oil temperatures and charge batteries, keeping the prime mover warm and ready to restart in cold weather at any location.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: warming a locomotive prime mover before a run. tasks.label: Operate locomotives in emergency situations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Road train on a signaled mainline: a hazard appears ahead (vehicle or trespasser at a grade crossing, obstruction, livestock, a stop indication being approached too fast). The crew member at the controls must sound the horn and put the train into emergency, handling the locomotive to stop as fast as the equipment allows without piling up the train, then notify the dispatcher.

Engineer becomes incapacitated or otherwise unable to operate (medical event, injury, falls asleep). The firer/conductor takes the throttle and brake, brings the loaded train to a controlled stop clear of crossings and bridges, secures it with air and hand brakes, and calls the dispatcher for help.

Yard, industrial plant lead, or port terminal switching emergency: during a shove or kick move a person, vehicle, or piece of equipment fouls the track, a cut of cars rolls away, or the movement threatens to run through a switch or strike standing cars. The operator (often working from the ground with a remote-control beltpack) must immediately stop and hold the movement.

Air-brake emergency on the road: undesired emergency application, parted air hose, or break-in-two on a grade. The operator must handle the locomotive to keep slack stretched and hold the train, then after the cause is found recharge the trainline, make the recoupling move, and restart the heavy train on grade without a second separation.

Incident/hazard response taken as found: derailment behind the locomotive, fire or hazmat release, washout or flooded track, or a crossing blocked in front of arriving emergency responders. The operator must move or hold the locomotive under non-standard conditions, cut cars away, and coordinate face-to-face and by radio with the dispatcher, responders, and ground crew.

tasks.label: Ride atop cars that have been shunted, and turn handwheels to control speeds or stop cars at specified positions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Flat-switching classification yard, normal daytime conditions: a car or short cut is kicked/dropped down a yard track; the brake operator rides on the car and works the handwheel brake to control the roll, stopping it clear of the switch or coupling it gently (about 4 mph) onto standing cars at the designated spot.

Same flat-yard car riding under adverse conditions: night, rain, snow or ice, cold, wind, a stiff or poorly maintained handbrake, cars of widely varying weight and rollability, uneven yard track and debris; the operator judges speed by feel and must stop the car accurately without damaging lading.

Hump or gravity classification yard: cars shunted over the crest roll into bowl tracks; the operator rides cars down the grade (or catches stalled cars in the bowl during trim work) and applies the handwheel to hold speed down and stop each car at the required position in the track.

Industrial customer facility (grain elevator, plant, mine load-out, bulk terminal, dumper): a car is dropped or shoved-and-cut down a spur inside the customer's premises; the operator rides it and brakes with the handwheel to stop it precisely at a loading spout, dock door, scale or dumper position, then ties the brake to hold it.

Remote/rural spur or street-running industrial trackage taken as found: gravity drop on a graded, weed-grown or paved-in siding with grade crossings, parked vehicles and unknown obstructions; the operator rides the car, controls speed on the grade with the handwheel, stops it at a spot marked only by a chalk mark or the customer's instruction, and secures it.

instances.label: Flat switching in a Class I/regional classification yard: yard conductor/foreman works on the ground alongside the switch engine (or with an RCL beltpack), reads a switch list, lines hand-throw and power switches, pulls cut levers to separate cuts of mixed manifest cars (boxcars, tanks, hoppers), kicks/shoves cars into designated tracks, couples cuts, rides cars, protects the shove point, sets and releases handbrakes. Day and night, all weather.

Hump-yard breakup of inbound trains: hump conductor/pin puller walks the crest uncoupling cuts by cut lever as the train is shoved over the hump; yardmaster directs the hump engine and trim engine; retarders and powered switches route cars into bowl tracks; trim crew pulls cars back and doubles bowl tracks together.

Departure-yard train makeup: doubling two or three yard tracks together into an outbound consist, coupling the cuts, lacing air hoses and opening angle cocks between every cut, releasing handbrakes, charging the trainline and performing the initial terminal air brake test, then verifying the consist against the train list before release.

Road freight conductor performing an en-route setout/pickup at a customer's industry track, small-town siding or interchange: cutting cars off the train, lining the switch, shoving into the spur past crossings and debris, spotting cars at loading spots, tying handbrakes, recoupling the train, lacing air and doing a set-and-release test. Site layouts vary widely; weather, darkness, grade crossings and public access are routine.

Industrial plant, transload or port terminal switching (plant railroad / short line crew): pulling loaded cars from loading spots and spotting empties inside the facility, working around plant equipment and gates, uncoupling and coupling conventional freight cars, moving cuts through derails and hand-throw switches, and assembling an outbound cut for interchange.

Passenger/commuter coach-yard consist changes: conductor/yardmaster directing an engineer or hostler to add or remove coaches, MU units or a locomotive from a trainset in a maintenance/coach yard, including coupling, connecting/verifying trainline connections, brake test and consist verification before the set is released to service.

tasks.label: Arrange for the removal of defective cars from trains at stations or stops.

instances.label: Road freight conductor sets out a bad-order car en route: at a siding or station stop, walks the consist (often at night, in rain/snow, on ballast), confirms the defect (hot bearing, broken air hose, dragging brake rigging, shifted load), radios the dispatcher and the mechanical desk for authority and a setout location, closes angle cocks and parts the glad hands, pulls the cut lever, lines hand-throw switches, shoves the car into the siding, applies a hand brake to secure it, recouples and re-charges the train, performs the required brake test and files the bad-order paperwork.

Yard conductor/foreman in a classification or terminal yard pulls cars flagged bad-order (by carmen or an inspection portal) out of an inbound cut and spots them on the RIP/repair track: uses a remote-control locomotive, cuts air, pulls pins, lines yard switches, shoves the car to the repair track, ties handbrakes, applies a bad-order tag and updates the car-management system before the train is rebuilt.

Yardmaster receives a bad-order report on a car in a train ready to depart and arranges its removal: decides where the car will be set out, assigns a crew and track, coordinates with the mechanical department and the train dispatcher, gives switching instructions by radio, and confirms the car has actually been pulled and the train re-blocked and re-tested before departure.

Local/industrial job at a customer's plant, elevator or transload track: conductor finds a defective car during a pickup (leaking load, defective wheel, damaged coupler), arranges to leave it behind or shove it to a designated bad-order spot; hand-throw switches and derails, uneven footing, plant vehicles and personnel moving nearby, limited radio coverage.

Passenger/commuter conductor at a station or terminal with a defective car in the consist (door or brake fault, HVAC failure): secures and locks out the car, moves passengers, notifies the control center and mechanical forces, and arranges for the car to be cut out of the consist or the trainset swapped at the coach yard, with the physical uncoupling (MU cables, air lines, drawbars) done on shop tracks.

It does not transfer, because the cars carry no knuckle couplers or brake pipe hoses to part and the system does not identify, tag, or secure a defective conventional railcar.

instances.label: Flat/classification yard switching: a yard conductor or switchman walks the ladder tracks and throws ground-mounted hand-throw switch stands (dozens, often 100+ per shift) to line each move, unlatching and re-latching levers, verifying points are closed, then signaling the engineer. Outdoors on ballast, day and night, all weather, with locomotives and cars moving nearby.

Road freight conductor working an industrial spur or siding: train stops on the main or branch track, conductor dismounts, unlocks the switch padlock, throws the hand switch and any derail, lines the route into the customer's track, then restores and locks the switch after the move. Remote trackside locations, layout differs at each industry.

Yardmaster or yard control operator in a tower/yard office: operates a control console (or radio/DTMF handheld) to activate power switch machines and yard/interlocking signals, lining entrance and exit routes for inbound, outbound, hump and trim moves according to the switch list and train plan.

Industrial plant, port terminal or short-line trackage: crew activates a mix of hand-throw switches, local control panels and radio-controlled power switches, plus derails, plant gates and warning/traffic signals, while spotting cars inside a plant or terminal with vehicle and pedestrian traffic around the track.

Degraded conditions: points fouled by packed snow, ice or ballast, a stiff/rusty or misaligned switch stand needing extra force and clearing, or hand-cranking a dual-control power switch after a machine, power or signal-system failure, then verifying and reporting the alignment.

tasks.label: Inspect freight cars for compliance with sealing procedures, and record car numbers and seal numbers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Classification/departure yard, daylight, dry conditions: conductor or yard crew walks a standing cut of 30-100 loaded boxcars and covered hoppers, confirms each door/hatch seal is present and unbroken and matches the switch list, and records car initials/number plus seal number on a paper list or handheld terminal.

Same yard walk under adverse conditions: at night with a lantern, or in rain, snow, heat or wind; footing on ballast between tracks, grimy/faded reporting marks, seals partly obscured by ice, mud or dunnage; car and seal numbers still must be read and recorded accurately.

Customer's industrial plant or private siding (grain elevator, auto plant, chemical works, warehouse dock): crew verifies that shipper-applied seals on outbound loads are intact and correct before pulling the cars, notes doors/hatches closed, and records car and seal numbers for the waybill/switch list.

Intermodal ramp or inbound interchange/receiving yard: seals on arriving cars, containers or trailers are checked against the manifest, exceptions (missing, broken, mismatched or re-applied seals) are flagged and documented with car/container number and seal number, sometimes for customs or security-sensitive traffic.

Remote industrial spur, team track, or a setout stop on the road: a handful of cars in a location taken as found - overgrown vegetation, mud or gravel, no lighting or fixed infrastructure; conductor checks seals on the cars being lifted or set out and records the numbers.

sources.system: Duos Technologies rip Railcar Inspection Portal
sources.title: 13 Duos Railcar Inspection Portals across US | Latest Railway News
sources.claim: Duos Technologies' rip Railcar Inspection Portal, a trackside machine-vision gantry, is deployed at 13 locations on the North American rail network and had performed millions of full railcar scans, imaging every car as trains pass at track speed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (automated railcar condition inspection) transfers: the portal images each passing car at high resolution in the same yard/mainline setting and produces a per-car record, which is the imaging and identification backbone the seal check requires.

sources.system: Duos Technologies rip Railcar Inspection Portal

sources.claim: The Duos portal automatically ties each captured image set to a specific railcar using the car's AEI tag / consist data, so each inspected car is identified and indexed by car number without human input.
sources.transferJustification: Directly substantiates the 'record car numbers' half of the task: the machine identifies and logs each car automatically as it passes the purpose-built portal.

sources.system: Duos rip portal AI (NVIDIA T4 servers)
sources.title: Duos Technologies Uses AI-Powered System for Railcar Inspection | NVIDIA Blog
sources.claim: Duos' AI analyzes portal imagery on-site to detect car conditions including open doors, running on GPU servers in the portal building.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (automated defect detection on passing freight cars) transfers to sealing compliance: detecting open/unsecured doors on a passing boxcar is the same perception problem class as confirming a door is closed and sealed.

instances.label: Road freight conductor, en route or at a setout point: a defect is reported or detected (dragging equipment, air hose, hot bearing alarm). The conductor directs the crew member/utility employee and coordinates with the mechanical desk and dispatcher on what must be checked and repaired, confirms the work was done and the car is safe or must be bad-ordered, and authorizes movement. Purpose served by instruction, verification and authorization.

Yardmaster in a classification yard: assigns car inspectors/mechanical forces to inbound and outbound tracks, ensures blue-flag protection is applied and released, sequences inspection and repair work against departure times, and confirms with the mechanical foreman that trains have been inspected and are release-ready before calling a crew.

Conductor at an initial terminal or after a pickup: directs the brakeman/utility worker positions for the air brake test and roll-by inspection, tells them what to check (set/release, hand brakes, angle cocks), receives and evaluates their reports, resolves discrepancies, and records/certifies the test as complete.

Passenger or commuter conductor at a station/terminal: supervises assistant conductors and coordinates with on-site mechanical staff over defective doors, HVAC, brakes or couplers on a consist; decides whether to cut out equipment, hold the train, or run with restrictions, and communicates the outcome to crew and control center.

Short line, industrial plant or transit yard conductor overseeing a trainee or utility employee performing routine equipment checks: briefs on what to inspect, observes and coaches, reviews the reported findings and defect paperwork, and follows up on corrections with the plant/mechanical department.

tasks.label: Inspect each car periodically during runs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Freight road conductor performs a roll-by inspection en route: from the cab, rear of train, or the ground at a meet/siding, watching the passing consist for hot or smoking journals, sticking or smoking brakes, dragging equipment, shifted lading, open doors/hatches, leaking loads, and running-gear problems, at 5-30 mph in any weather, day or ..., anywhere along the mainline right-of-way.

Conductor walks the train mid-route after a defect-detector alarm, undesired emergency brake application, or reported problem: dismounts onto ballast along the mainline (curves, bridges, grade crossings, remote terrain, mud/snow), walks car by car checking wheels, bearings, brake rigging, couplers, air hoses, and load security to locate the defect and report its car/axle location.

Conductor inspects the consist at the initial terminal or yard before/at the start of a run: walks the standing train on a yard track, checking each car for obvious defects, securement, brake application/release during the air test, and load or door condition, in a railroad-controlled yard with fixed track layout and lighting.

Passenger/commuter conductor walks through each car during the run: checks doors, vestibules, HVAC, lighting, restrooms, emergency equipment, unusual noises or smells, and passenger-related hazards while the train is moving and occupied.

Yard/industrial-plant switch crew conductor checks cars being handled during switching moves: rides or walks alongside cuts of cars in a plant or yard, spotting hand brakes still applied, damaged couplers or air hoses, shifted or leaking loads, and improper placards before the cars are moved or spotted.

tasks.label: Operate controls to open and close transit vehicle doors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine revenue station stop on a heavy-rail subway/elevated line (grade-separated right-of-way, high-level platforms): operator berths the train at the stop mark, selects the correct side, operates the door controls to open, observes boarding/alighting via cab window, platform mirrors or CCTV, then closes the doors, confirms the door-closed-and-locked indication, and releases the train. Dozens of repetitions per run.

Routine stop on a street-running streetcar or light-rail line: vehicle stops at a curbside or median island stop in mixed traffic, operator enables/opens the doors (often with passenger-actuated door buttons), watches boarding amid pedestrians, cyclists and passing cars, then closes doors before proceeding.

Peak-hour or crowded stop where the door cycle is contested: passengers block the doorway or hold doors, a bag/coat/stroller is caught, doors fail to lock; operator re-opens, makes an announcement, and re-cycles the doors, sometimes repeatedly, until a clear closed-and-locked indication is obtained.

Accessible boarding: opening doors for a wheelchair, scooter or walker user, holding the doors open longer, and — on light rail with high-block platforms or low-floor stops — operating the control that deploys the bridge plate/ramp, then retracting it and closing the doors after boarding.

Non-standard door operation: selective door opening at short platforms or platforms serving only part of the train, correct-side enabling at island/side platform combinations, opening a single door for fare-handling or crew access, and door operation at terminals, yards and on non-revenue moves.

Abnormal or emergency door work: a door faults and must be isolated/cut out and locked out of service, manual/emergency door release is used, a passenger or object is trapped as the train starts, or doors must be opened to the trackbed or between cars for an evacuation or a mid-tunnel incident.

tasks.label: Drive and control rail-guided public transportation, such as subways, elevated trains, and electric-powered streetcars, trams, or trolleys, to transport passengers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Normal revenue run on a fully grade-separated heavy-rail subway/elevated line (NYC subway, Chicago 'L', WMATA, MARTA, BART, MBTA Red/Orange/Blue, SEPTA, PATH): terminal-to-terminal trip on schedule, observing wayside or cab signals and speed restrictions, berthing precisely at open platforms with no platform screen doors, operating passenger doors, watching platform edge during boarding, relaying/reversing at terminals.

Heavy-rail run under degraded or abnormal conditions: driving in restricted/manual mode past failed signals or during signal-system outages, crawling and single-tracking through flagged work zones on hand signals from track workers, emergency braking for trespassers or debris, holding for a sick passenger or door problem, wrong-rail moves and reroutes ordered by the rail control center.

Light-rail run on semi-exclusive right-of-way (Denver RTD, DART, Portland MAX, Salt Lake TRAX, LA A Line, Seattle Link surface segments): 35-65 mph on private ROW between low-platform stations, gated at-grade road crossings and traffic-signal-controlled crossings, watching for gate-runners, trespassers and pedestrians at crossings, sounding horn/bell, keeping headway.

Street-running streetcar or light-rail surface branch in mixed traffic (Portland Streetcar, Cincinnati, Kansas City, Boston Green Line surface, SF Muni surface, Philadelphia trolleys): shares travel lanes with cars, obeys traffic signals, stops at curbside islands, negotiates jaywalkers, cyclists, left-turning traffic and double-parked vehicles fouling the track, makes turns through busy intersections.

Heritage/vintage operation: San Francisco cable cars (grip and track brakes, manual gripping on hills), New Orleans and other PCC/heritage streetcars with legacy manual controllers, running in street traffic among tourist crowds, with hand-operated equipment and frequent standing loads.

tasks.label: Regulate vehicle speed and the time spent at each stop to maintain schedules.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Heavy-rail subway operator on a legacy fixed-block signalled line (e.g. most of the NYC subway, Chicago 'L', Boston): manually notching power and brake between stations to signal/timetable speeds, judging the station stop, then shortening or extending dwell according to platform crowding and control-centre instructions to hold the schedule. Setting: agency-owned tunnels, elevated structure and staffed stations.

Subway or elevated line equipped with CBTC/ATO (NYC L and 7, WMATA Metrorail, BART): operator engages automatic mode so the train runs the commanded speed profile and berths at the platform, then operator opens/closes doors and releases the train, trimming dwell to hold headway. Setting: agency-controlled grade-separated railway and platforms.

Light rail / elevated suburban train on exclusive or semi-exclusive right-of-way with protected grade crossings, curves, outdoor weather (rain, snow, heat restrictions): regulating speed to civil and crossing restrictions and controlling dwell at platform stops to stay on the timetable. Setting: agency-owned right-of-way and stations.

Streetcar or light rail running in mixed street traffic (Portland Streetcar, SF Muni surface, New Orleans, Toronto-style): pacing the car to road traffic and traffic signals, braking for jaywalkers and turning cars, stopping at curbside/island stops and managing dwell for boarding, all while trying to hold a published headway. Setting: public street shared with cars and pedestrians.

Disrupted or degraded service: running slow orders or single-tracking, recovering a late schedule, holding at a station to fill a gap or make a connection, crush-load boarding that stretches dwell, adverse weather; speed and dwell are adjusted continuously under control-centre direction. Setting: agency-controlled subway/light-rail line.

tasks.label: Direct emergency evacuation procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Heavy-rail rapid transit (subway/elevated): a train is taken out of service for an emergency at or near a station (smoke condition, fire alarm, brake/door failure, police or medical incident). The operator coordinates by radio with the control center, brings the train to the platform, opens doors, makes repeated PA announcements directing passengers off, walks the cars to confirm no one remains, assists elderly/disabled riders onto the platform, and secures the train.

Subway train stalled between stations; controlled detrainment into the tunnel. Operator confirms with control center that third rail is de-energized and traffic stopped, opens the emergency detrainment door or side doors, deploys the emergency ladder/ramp to the trackbed or bench walkway, then leads several hundred passengers by flashlight along a dark, narrow walkway to the nearest emergency exit or station, keeping them clear of the third rail and controlling panic.

Catastrophic incident: derailment, collision, or heavy smoke/fire with injured passengers, loss of lighting and communications, damaged or blocked doors, debris on the trackbed, and passengers already self-evacuating. Operator must improvise an egress route, triage who can walk, hold the crowd back from an energized third rail, and hand off to arriving fire/EMS.

Street-running streetcar/light rail: collision with an automobile, onboard fire, overhead-wire or medical/security emergency in mixed traffic. Operator opens doors or emergency exits, directs passengers off onto a live roadway or sidewalk, moves them clear of traffic and downed wire, deploys the ramp for a wheelchair rider, and keeps the group together until supervisors arrive.

Evacuation from an elevated structure or aerial guideway: passengers detrained onto a narrow emergency walkway at height, or brought down an emergency ladder/stair to street level, in wind, heat, or rain, with riders reluctant or physically unable to climb down.

Scheduled emergency evacuation drills and recertification exercises at a training facility, yard, or closed section of line, with volunteer 'passengers' and safety observers. The operator runs the full announced procedure end-to-end - power removal request, door/detrainment device operation, ladder deployment, crowd marshalling to a point of safety - and is graded on it.

sources.title: The Automatic System GoA4 - thessmetro.gr
sources.claim: Thessaloniki Metro is a deployed GoA4 (unattended) driverless metro with platform screen doors; its published evacuation procedure states that when a train must be evacuated, trained human personnel guide passengers along the tunnel walkway to the nearest station and stay with wheelchair users. The automation drives the train but does not direct the evacuation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is fully automatic train driving and door operation in a purpose-built, screen-doored metro. It does not transfer to 'direct emergency evacuation procedures': the operator's evacuation duties (detraining, escorting, assisting the mobility impaired) are explicitly assigned to human personnel even in this most machine-adapted rail environment.

sources.developer: Transport for NSW / Metro Trains Sydney
sources.title: Safety when travelling by metro and train | transportnsw.info
sources.claim: Sydney Metro is a deployed driverless (GoA4) metro with no operator on board; official passenger safety guidance says that in an emergency or evacuation passengers must follow instructions from a human Customer Journey Coordinator or from staff in the Operations Control Centre, i.e. evacuations are directed by people, not by the automated train.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is unattended automatic train operation on a sealed guideway. Capability does not carry over to directing an evacuation: the operator's evacuation role is filled by dispatched human coordinators and control-centre staff.

sources.transferJustification: Related task is driverless train operation in an institution-controlled guideway. It does not substantiate directing evacuations, which this operator still staffs with human attendants who travel to the incident.

sources.system: Evacuation guide robot (Robinette/Wagner robot-guided evacuation experiments)
sources.developer: Penn State / Georgia Tech Research Institute (Alan R. Wagner et al.)
sources.title: Robot-Guided Evacuation as a Paradigm for Human-Robot Interaction Research (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: Robot-guided emergency evacuation exists only as human-subject research: an autonomous mobile guide robot shepherds individual participants toward exits in a university laboratory building with sham emergencies (smoke machines). Compliance was 75% at best and fell below 12% when a crowd fled the other way after a robot mistake - far below the reliability an employer would accept.
sources.transferJustification: This is the closest related task (a robot directing people to an exit during an emergency). It fails to transfer: experiments are in a flat, mapped office building with single subjects, involve no train detrainment, ladders, third-rail hazard, or verification that cars are empty, and compliance rates are far below worker quality.

sources.transferJustification: Related tasks are passenger wayfinding and platform patrol in the same E2 setting (a metro station). They do not transfer to directing an emergency evacuation: no demonstrated ability to open or secure train doors, deploy detrainment equipment, marshal a panicked crowd, or confirm cars are clear, and the deployment is framed as supporting human staff.

tasks.label: Handle lines to moor vessels to wharfs, to tie up vessels to other vessels, or to rig towing lines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled ferry/RoPax/passenger-vessel deckhand handling mooring lines at a fixed terminal berth, many times per shift: heaving/passing eyes over standard bollards, working a fixed berth with known fenders and ramp, passengers boarding, short turnarounds.

Able seaman on an ocean, coastal or Great Lakes merchant ship mooring the ship to a commercial terminal wharf: heaving line, messenger, winch-drawn head/stern lines and springs onto bollards, doubling up, tending lines for tide and draft change, and securing the vessel in lock chambers en route.

Inland towboat deckhand making up, shifting and breaking a barge tow: face wires, ratchets and cheater pipes, coupling barges to each other and to the boat, catching lines in fleeting areas and checking the tow with lines on lock walls; night, weather, mud, moving equipment underfoot.

Harbor or ocean tug deckhand rigging and handling towing lines to another vessel underway: catching the heaving line from a ship's centre lead, hauling the messenger and towline, making fast and letting go on the tow staple/bitts, rigging and recovering bridles and tow wire on a coastal tow.

Tying a vessel up to another vessel: making a tug fast to a barge in a notch or on the hip with facing wires, bringing a bunker or lightering barge alongside a ship, or rafting up - with fenders, swell and changing relative freeboard.

Small utility craft - crew boats, tour boats, OSVs, dredge tenders, research and government vessels - tying up at assorted piers, floating docks, dolphins, mooring buoys or offshore structures with varied hardware and often no shore line handlers.

tasks.label: Stand watch in ships' bows or bridge wings to look for obstructions in a ship's path or to locate navigational aids, such as buoys or lighthouses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Deep-sea merchant vessel on open-ocean passage at night: an AB stands lookout on the bridge wing or in the wheelhouse, scanning the 360-degree horizon by sight and hearing, and reports lights, vessels, and large floating objects to the officer of the watch by relative bearing.

Coastal or harbor approach in congested traffic or restricted visibility (fog, rain, glare): a seaman is posted as bow lookout, reporting buoys, range lights, lighthouses, small craft, fishing gear, and floating debris, plus fog signals heard, immediately to the bridge.

Inland/coastal towing vessel, tug-and-barge, or workboat on rivers and the Intracoastal Waterway: a deckhand stands watch forward of a long tow or in the pilothouse, calling out channel buoys, day marks, bridge piers, logs, and recreational boats to the pilot.

Passenger ferry or harbor vessel during departure, transit, and docking: a sailor stands lookout on the bow or bridge wing watching for swimmers, kayaks, small craft crossing the track, and obstructions at the slip, and reports to the master.

Anchor watch or standby lookout while anchored, drifting, or maneuvering in a traffic separation scheme: the seaman monitors for dragging anchor, approaching vessels, and shifting navigational aid bearings and reports observations to the mate.

tasks.label: Splice and repair ropes, wire cables, or cordage, using marlinespikes, wire cutters, twine, and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Able seaman makes an eye splice in a three-strand or 12-strand synthetic mooring line on the main deck of a merchant vessel, tug or supply boat: unlays or opens the rope, forms the eye to a specified size around a thimble, tucks strands with a fid/marlinespike, tapers and buries the tail, then whips or stitches the throat. Line is 1-3 inches diameter, stiff, sometimes wet and salt-encrusted; work is done at a bollard, capstan or on deck with hand tools.

Repair of a chafed or damaged section of running gear or mooring line in the boatswain's locker/deck workshop or on deck alongside: cutting out the bad section with a knife or hot knife, joining with a short/long splice or re-terminating both parts, renewing chafe gear, seizing and whipping the ends with twine so the line can be returned to service.

Small cordage and marlinespike work: putting sail-twine whippings and seizings on line ends, making up lashings, gantlines, heaving lines with a monkey's fist, net or canvas lacing, servings on standing rigging — done at a bench in the deck workshop or seated on deck, with many small varied jobs and no standard workpiece.

Wire cable work: cutting damaged wire rope with wire cutters after seizing the cut on both sides, re-terminating a cargo gear runner, guy, or lifeboat/davit fall with a hand-tucked splice or a Flemish eye and swaged/bulldog-clipped termination, and repairing/serving broken-wire areas — heavy, springy, greasy 6x19/6x37 wire aboard ship.

Emergency or underway repair: a parted mooring or towing line, a fouled or damaged tail/pennant re-spliced at sea or during a job, on a moving deck in wind, spray or at night, with the line partly under load or awkwardly led, and a short deadline before the next maneuver.

sources.title: TieBot: Learning to Knot a Tie from Visual Demonstration through a Real-to-Sim-to-Real Approach
sources.claim: State of the art in autonomous dual-arm manipulation of flexible linear objects: a dual-arm robot learned to knot a necktie from visual demonstration, succeeding in 5 of 10 real-world trials in a lab setup.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: knotting a flexible linear object with two arms — the nearest robotic capability to rope splicing. It is cited as a ceiling, not a positive: a 50% lab success rate on a soft, thin, unloaded tie is far below the reliability and strength-critical precision required for a marine eye splice in stiff 1-3 inch rope.

sources.system: Dual-arm two-finger robot in-air knotting system
sources.title: In-air Knotting of Rope using Dual-Arm Robot based on Deep Learning (arXiv:2103.09402)
sources.claim: Autonomous in-air knotting of rope by a dual-arm two-finger robot using deep learning, demonstrated on a laboratory bench with a single rope type.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: forming knots in rope. Transfer is limited — knotting manipulates the whole rope, while splicing requires unlaying individual strands, opening the lay with a marlinespike/fid and tucking strands under tension; no cited system performs the latter, so this evidence bounds rather than substantiates capability.

sources.title: Eye & Eye Wire Rope Slings for Lifting | Holloway Houston

sources.title: New 400t-swager for wire rope | WIRE

tasks.label: Operate, maintain, or repair ship equipment, such as winches, cranes, derricks, or weapons system.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Berthing/unberthing alongside a terminal berth or in a lock: run out heaving and mooring lines through fairleads, make fast on bitts, operate mooring winches to heave the vessel alongside, set tension and brakes, then slack and let go on departure. Deck crew work on the forecastle/poop with linesmen ashore.

Other deck-gear operation at sea and at anchor: operating the windlass to let go and weigh anchor and securing with stoppers/devil's claw, opening and closing hatch covers and cargo access equipment, rigging pilot and accommodation ladders, handling tug and towing gear, swinging out and testing lifeboat davits during drills, often on a moving deck in wind and spray.

Repetitive bulk cargo discharge with the ship's own grab cranes on a geared bulk carrier or self-unloader: cycling the crane between hold and quayside hopper, trimming the pile, clearing hold corners, over many hours alongside a berth.

Rigged lifts with ship's cranes and derricks: hooking slings, strops and lifting frames to stores, spares, pallets, project cargo, containers or offshore supply loads; guiding and tending the load with tag lines; landing, unhooking, and lashing/securing on deck.

Preventive maintenance and corrective repair of deck machinery and engine-room auxiliaries: greasing winch and crane bearings, lubricating and slushing wires, topping up and changing hydraulic and lube oil, changing filters and cleaning strainers, testing and adjusting winch brakes, plus repairs such as renewing wire rope on a drum, replacing hoses, seals, brake linings, motors and pumps, in cramped, oily, corroded spaces.

Weapons-system operation aboard armed vessels (naval, Coast Guard, Military Sealift Command): manning a gun mount or close-in weapons station, standing ready, tracking and engaging surface/air threats or targets during exercises.

tasks.label: Sweep, mop, and wash down decks to remove oil, dirt, and debris, using brooms, mops, brushes, and hoses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine washdown of large, open, machine-traversable deck areas on big vessels (cruise promenade/pool decks, ferry vehicle decks, wide unobstructed stretches of main deck): removing salt spray, dirt and litter with scrubbers, brooms and deck-wash hoses while the vessel is in service.

Washdown of obstructed working deck areas on cargo ships and tankers: hosing and brooming salt, rust scale and cargo residue around hatch coamings, winches, bitts, pipework and gutter bars, into corners and scuppers, and hosing down bulwarks and hatch tops.

Cleaning oil off the deck after cargo or bunkering operations on a tanker/OSV: degreaser, absorbent pads, stiff brushes and hose at the manifold, drip trays and save-alls, in tight pipework, with scuppers plugged so no oil goes overboard.
Interior housekeeping aboard: sweeping and mopping accommodation alleyways, mess room and stairways/ladderways, over raised door coamings, around furniture, lockers and fittings.

Engine room / machinery space deck plates and gratings: mopping and degreasing oil and soot from steel plates, catwalks and bilge plates in a hot, noisy, confined space crowded with pipes, machinery and vertical ladders.

Washing down the deck of a small working vessel underway or alongside (tug, fishing boat, small ferry, supply boat): hosing catch residue, mud, grease and fuel drips off a cluttered deck full of gear and lines, on a pitching, slippery platform in weather.

sources.title: Cleaning robots | Kärcher International
sources.claim: The Kärcher KIRA B 50 ... a commercially sold autonomous scrubber-dryer that cleans medium and large hard-floor areas unattended, with a docking station that refills fresh water, empties dirty water and recharges it.
sources.transferJustification: Wet scrubbing/mopping of hard floors, including narrow corridors, is the mop-and-wash element of the task; the docking station makes the cycle unattended.

tasks.label: Lubricate machinery, equipment, or engine parts, such as gears, shafts, or bearings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Merchant ship engine room round: oiler walks the machinery spaces checking sump levels and sight glasses on main/auxiliary engines, purifiers, pumps and compressors, tops up lube oil from cans or hoses, hand-greases pump and motor bearings at zerk fittings with a grease gun, oils linkages, wipes excess and logs readings. Hot, cramped, vibrating space, machinery running, vessel moving at sea.

Deck machinery greasing on a merchant vessel: mooring winches, windlass, capstans, deck crane slew bearing and sheaves, hatch cover wheels and cleats, watertight door dogs. Grease gun rounds at dozens of exposed fittings, outdoors in spray, rain and cold, on a rolling deck, some points aloft or in tight recesses.

Wire rope and open-gear/exposed-surface lubrication: dressing mooring and crane wires with rope grease while spooling, brushing or spraying grease on open gear teeth, davit tracks, lifeboat gear, gangway and pilot ladder hardware, threaded spindles and screw jacks.

Steering gear, stern tube and shaft line service: check and top up steering gear reservoir and stern tube header tank oil, grease rudder carrier, stern gland and thruster points, check intermediate shaft bearing oil rings and sight glasses, watch for leaks after topping up.

Small-vessel work (tug, inland towboat, ferry, OSV, workboat): deckhand/oiler greases towing winch, capstan, shaft coupling and stuffing box, tops up main engine, generator and reduction gear oil in a cramped engine room with older, non-standard equipment, often while underway or between short runs.

sources.system: DOPAG production cell for automated grease metering (6-axis robot + lubriLine pump, spray and shot valves)
sources.title: Production cell for automated grease metering | DOPAG
sources.claim: A commercial production cell uses a 6-axis articulated robot that picks gearwheels from workpiece carriers and presents them to spray and shot valves that apply grease to the inside and outside of ... gears, with metered flow control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: greasing gears in manufacturing. Same physical act as the oiler's greasing of gears and bearings (metered grease applied to gear teeth and bores), but with the part fixtured on a carrier and presented to the robot, i.e. an E1 presentation of the work.

sources.system: SP Automation robotic oil filling system (Fanuc M-10iD/12)
sources.title: Robotic Oil Filling System - Automation | SP Automation & Robotics
sources.claim: A deployed industrial cell uses a Fanuc six-axis robot that automatically couples to filling tooling and pumps predetermined, metered volumes of oil into product reservoirs, with barcode identification and load-cell verification of fill weight.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: filling oil reservoirs in production. Equivalent to the oiler's topping-up of sumps and reservoirs to a specified quantity, including verification of the amount delivered, when the unit is presented to the robot on a pallet/fixture.

sources.system: Graco Trabon LubeMaster multi-pump progressive automatic lubrication system with MSP/MXP divider valves
sources.title: A Lubrication System for Cranes in Harsh Weather | Graco
sources.claim: Ship-to-shore container cranes in coastal ports are fitted with automatic progressive lubrication systems that deliver grease from pumps through divider blocks to up to 300 grease points ..., with over 100 crane installations completed, operating in harsh outdoor weather.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: greasing crane slew bearings, sheaves and pins. Same objects, grease types and weather exposure as shipboard deck crane and winch greasing; the grease points are hard-plumbed to metering blocks, i.e. the work is brought to the machine (E1 presentation).

sources.system: SKF/Lincoln centralized automatic lubrication systems for marine equipment

sources.claim: SKF/Lincoln market and supply centralized automatic lubrication systems specifically for marine equipment, delivering grease to winch drive lubrication ... operates, and covering propeller shaft bearings, steering gears, ropes and cables.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: open-gear lubrication in industrial plant. Same lubricant and same exposed gear/track surfaces as shipboard open gears, davit tracks and screw jacks, with the nozzle fixed relative to the gear (E1 presentation).

sources.system: MAN B&W Alpha Lubricator / Alpha ACC cylinder lubrication system
sources.date: in service since circa 1998; article dated June 2026

sources.claim: Modern two-stroke marine main engines aboard ships use an electronically controlled cylinder lubrication system ... meters and injects cylinder oil onto liner surfaces automatically at defined crank positions, replacing manually adjusted mechanical lubricators.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: engine-part lubrication aboard ship. Shows lubricant delivery to running engine parts is automated on vessels when the delivery path is engineered into the machine, which is the E1 form of the instance.

sources.system: Boston Dynamics Spot with Autowalk / Spot Arm
sources.title: Automated Inspections Made Simple | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: The state of the art for autonomous mobile robots in industrial facilities is autonomous inspection missions along taught routes, with arm use limited to actions such as opening doors; no lubrication service work is offered.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound, not support: the leading mobile manipulator deployed in structured facilities performs inspection and door opening, not locating grease fittings, coupling a grease gun or topping up sumps, so E2 in-situ lubrication is unsubstantiated.

tasks.label: Chip and clean rust spots on decks, superstructures, or sides of ships, using wire brushes and hand or air chipping machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Able/ordinary seaman on a merchant vessel underway at sea: spot-chipping rust streaks and scale on the weather deck — around hatch coamings, pad eyes, cleats, pipe runs, welds and bulwarks — with a needle gun and wire brush on a pitching, salt-wetted deck, feathering edges and sweeping up scale so a primer coat can go on the same watch.

Vessel in port or at anchor: chipping and wire-brushing rust on superstructure exteriors — deckhouse bulkheads, watertight doors, ladders, handrails, davits and vents — working from deck level, ladders or a rigged staging, with power/air chipping tools and hand scrapers, then wiping down and priming.

Interior spaces: rust chipping in the engine room bilges, tank tops, machinery flats, steering gear room, paint and bosun's stores — confined, poorly lit areas crowded with piping, cable runs, gratings and mounted machinery that must not be damaged; needle gun and hand wire brush, debris collected by hand.

Hull sides and freeboard: rust on the topsides, boot topping, anchor pocket, mooring/hawse areas and bulwark exteriors, worked over the side from a rigged stage or bosun's chair, from a workboat alongside, or from the pier while in port; wind, wave wash and access restrictions apply.

Enclosed-space work: chipping loose scale and rust off frames, brackets, girders and bulkheads in ballast tanks, void spaces and cargo holds between cargoes (bulk carrier hold cleaning/preservation), under enclosed-space entry permit with ventilation, staging or hold ladders.

sources.system: Blastman automatic blast cleaning robots (B-series, in 100 m x 30 m blast room)
sources.date: page retrieved 2026-07; systems in service since 2017
sources.title: Ship Building - Blastman Robotics Ltd
sources.claim: Blastman supplies automatic abrasive blast-cleaning robots that work inside enclosed shipyard blast rooms and blast-clean entire ship blocks and barges (rust, scale and old coating removal to a specified cleanliness/roughness grade) without scaffolding or man lifts.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic abrasive blast cleaning of ship steel in a blast room. It removes exactly the same corrosion products and old paint from the same substrate (ship plate, stiffeners, deck and hull structure) to the coating-ready standard a chipping/wire-brushing sailor is trying to reach; only the tool (grit blast vs. needle gun) differs.

sources.system: Blastman robotic blasting system at C&C Marine and Repair
sources.developer: Blastman Robotics Ltd / C&C Marine and Repair
sources.title: Ship Building - Blastman Robotics Ltd
sources.claim: A US barge builder/repairer (C&C Marine and Repair, Belle Chasse, USA) has run a Blastman robotic blasting system in production since 2017, cutting manual blasting time on a barge by 85%; the robots handle production and maintenance blasting of whole barges.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: whole-vessel (barge) blast cleaning in a purpose-built blast room, i.e. rust/coating removal from marine steel at yard-accepted quality, substituting directly for manual blasting labour of the kind sailors perform in spot form.

sources.system: GrayMatter Robotics Scan&Sand / GMR-AI robotic sanding cell
sources.title: A Robotic Sanding Cell in 'Putty Land' | Cutting Tool Engineering
sources.claim: Commercially deployed robotic sanding cells scan an arbitrary part placed in the cell and autonomously plan collision-free abrasive tool paths, removing material to a uniform finish without part-specific programming.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous abrasive surface preparation of variable-geometry workpieces inside a fenced cell. It shows that, when the workpiece is brought to the machine, contact abrasive removal on surfaces that differ unit-to-unit no longer needs teaching or teleoperation — the capability gap for E1 chipping/cleaning is closed by scanning plus automatic path planning.

sources.system: QXY-series steel plate preservation / shot blasting and priming line
sources.developer: ATHI Group (and similar shipyard plate-line suppliers)
sources.title: Mechanical Descaling | ATHI Group
sources.claim: Shipyards use conveyorized steel-plate preservation (shot-blasting) lines that automatically shot-blast rust and mill scale off plate and profiles and then apply shop primer, with the work presented to the machine on rollers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic rust removal from ship steel. Same substrate and same accepted output (bare, coating-ready steel), achieved with zero human intervention once the work is fed to the machine — the canonical E1 presentation of this work.

sources.system: WallHiker W-04 sandblasting robot / W-06 UHP hydroblasting magnetic crawler
sources.title: Ship Hull Cleaning & Blasting - AKA Robotics
sources.claim: Commercial magnetic-crawler blasting robots used on ship hulls in yards remove rust and paint but are driven by a human operator with a remote controller for both travel and blasting.
sources.transferJustification: Same task on the actual ship (E2 setting). Cited to show that the systems that do work on in-service/drydocked vessels are continuously teleoperated, so they cannot support a positive E2 judgment.

sources.title: Seaspan introduces new remote-controlled Dockboy surface prep vehicle - Marine Log
sources.claim: Seaspan's Dockboy, a tracked ultra-high-pressure surface-preparation vehicle used on hulls in its drydock, is remote-controlled by an operator; first commercial project use in late 2025.
sources.transferJustification: Same task in a drydock (E2 setting). Cited as negative evidence: the state of the art for hull surface preparation on real vessels is remote control, not autonomy.

sources.developer: Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) ROAR lab
sources.title: Hornbill: A Self-Evaluating Hydro-Blasting Reconfigurable Robot for Ship Hull Maintenance - IEEE Xplore
sources.claim: A research climbing robot, Hornbill, has been shown navigating autonomously on ship hull surfaces in drydock and water-jet blasting off coating/corrosion, with a neural-network scheme evaluating the cleanliness it achieved.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (corrosion/coating removal from a ship hull) in an E2 setting (drydock). Cited because it is the closest autonomous demonstration on a real vessel, but it is a laboratory/field prototype at patch scale with no evidence of completing a yard-accepted job.

tasks.label: Paint or varnish decks, superstructures, lifeboats, or sides of ships.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Weather-deck preservation aboard a merchant vessel in service: crew roll/brush deck paint over the main deck, hatch coamings, pad-eyes, pipe runs and around lashing gear after spot-priming rust patches; work done at sea or alongside, on a moving, cluttered steel deck exposed to weather and salt spray.

Superstructure exterior painting aboard a vessel: deckhouse bulkheads, funnel, mast, ladders, railings and doors coated by brush/roller (occasionally small spray gun) from deck level, staging or a bosun's chair, cutting in around windows, fittings and name markings, in port or at sea.

Hull side / freeboard touch-up while the ship is afloat: painting boot-topping and topsides rust streaks and scuffs from a stage, punt or pier with extension rollers, alongside a berth or at anchor, with wave motion, wind and limited access.

Full hull-side coating during a shipyard drydocking: the flat sides and freeboard are washed, blasted and recoated in dock, with crew assisting/supervising and hand-finishing edges and inaccessible areas.

Detail work on boats and fittings: lifeboats/rescue boats and davits, deck machinery housings, bitts and mooring gear given touch-up coats, plus varnishing brightwork (teak handrails, boat gunwales, wheelhouse trim) requiring a fine, sag-free finish.

Interior of the superstructure: accommodation passageways, storerooms, workshops and machinery-space bulkheads and deckheads brush/roller painted around piping, cable trays, valves and fittings while the vessel is in service.

sources.system: GreenDock Robot H28 (Autonomous Mobile Blast & Paint Robot)
sources.title: Greendock Robot H28 - AMBPR
sources.claim: AMBPR's GreenDock robot is a mobile nacelle-mounted multifunction shipyard robot that washes, blasts and applies paint to ship hulls, covering ~150 m2 areas autonomously while one operator monitors several machines.

sources.system: AMBPR Autonomous Mobile Blast & Paint Robot (GreenDock)
